safety_implication: Defines operational boundaries for evaluating fuel flammability and cool flame behavior under varying spacecraft atmospheric compositions.
evidence: The oxygen mole fraction will be varied in the range 0.18 to 0.35. The total pressure of the combustion chamber will be varied in the range 0.5 to 5.0 atm.
variables: Oxygen mole fraction and total pressure
earth_application: Controlled combustion and safety standard testing at various pressures and oxygen levels.

finding: Droplet lifetimes for n-heptane and methanol droplets burning in air at one atmospheric pressure range from 18 to 72 s for initial diameters of 3 to 6 mm.
safety_implication: Burn durations dictate the required observation time in microgravity facilities to capture complete combustion phenomena.
evidence: The values of τl for n-heptane, and methanol droplets burning in air at one atmospheric pressure range from 18 to 72 s for initial droplet diameters in the range 3 to 6 mm assuming an average burning rate constant of 0.5 mm^2/s.
other_measurements: droplet lifetime: 18 to 72 s
variables: Initial droplet size and fuel type
earth_application: Liquid fuel droplet combustion lifetime estimations.

finding: Test fuels must be research grade, dry, degassed, highest purity commercially available, with initial fuel temperature in the range of 18 to 27 C.
safety_implication: Ensures repeatability and precise baseline conditions for combustion and flammability testing in space missions.
evidence:
- research grade, dry, degassed, highest purity commercially available
- fuel temperature at the start of the test shall be in the range of 18 - 27 C
earth_application: Standardized laboratory fuel testing procedures.

finding: Droplet deployment size requirements specify a diameter of 2 mm to 6 mm plus or minus 0.25 mm, reproducible to within plus or minus 10 percent.
safety_implication: Strict control over initial droplet size is critical to maintain valid spherically symmetric models for fire safety design.
evidence: - 2 mm to 6 mm ± 0.25 mm and reproducible to within ± 10%
fuel_geometry: Spherical droplet, 2 mm to 6 mm diameter
earth_application: Droplet combustion experiment standards.

finding: Initial test pressures are required to be set at 0.5 to 3.0 atm (5.0 atm desired) plus or minus 0.05 atm, and maintained within plus or minus 10 percent throughout each test.
safety_implication: Maintains predictable combustion environments and containment safety bounds during testing.
evidence:
- test pressures at 0.5 - 3.0 (5.0, desired) atm ± 0.05 atm
- chamber pressure to be maintained within ± 10% of initial conditions throughout each test.
earth_application: High-pressure combustion test safety protocols.

finding: Microgravity acceleration levels are required to be between 2x10^-6 and 2x10^-4 depending on droplet size.
safety_implication: Ensures minimal buoyancy effects during spacecraft droplet combustion testing to accurately reflect microgravity fire behavior.
evidence: -acceleration levels are required to be 2_x_10^(_−_6) _−_2_x_10^(_−_4) on three axes depending on the size of the droplet
earth_application: Fundamental combustion research and droplet burning modeling.

finding: Fuel temperature prior to the start of any test must be in the range of 18 - 27 C.
safety_implication: Standardized initial fuel temperature ensures repeatability and prevents unpredictable ignition behavior in spacecraft experiments.
evidence: _Fuel Temperature:_ in the range of 18 - 27 _C_ prior to the start of any test.
earth_application: Standardized fuel handling protocols.

finding: Droplet diameter shall vary from 2 mm to 6 mm with reproducibility within plus or minus 10%.
safety_implication: Precise droplet sizing ensures consistent ignition and combustion testing for spacecraft fire safety hazard assessments.
evidence: _Droplet size:_ droplet diameter shall vary from 2 _mm_ to 6 _mm ±_ 0 _._ 25 _mm Droplet reproducibility:_ droplet size shall be reproducible to within _±_ 10%
earth_application: Droplet combustion analysis and spray burner safety.

finding: Initial ambient absolute pressure shall be set to 0.5 - 3.0 atm (necessary) or 0.5 - 5.0 atm (desired).
safety_implication: Enables evaluation of fire risks across varied spacecraft cabin pressure environments.
evidence: _Ambient_ _<u>pressure:</u>_ initial ambient absolute pressure shall be set to 0 _._ 5 _−_ 3 _._ 0 _atm_ (necessary), 0 _._ 5 _−_ 5 _._ 0 _atm_ (desired) _±_ 0 _._ 05 _atm_.
earth_application: High pressure combustion safety.

finding: Oxygen mole fraction shall range from 0.1 to 0.4 to study its influence on burning rate, extinction diameter, and flame chemistry.
safety_implication: Provides crucial flammability boundaries under different oxygen enrichment scenarios relevant to spacecraft atmospheres.
evidence: _Oxygen Mole Fraction:_ oxygen mole fraction shall range from 0 _._ 1 _−_ 0 _._ 4 _±_ 0 _._ 005.
earth_application: Oxygen-enriched industrial environments safety.

finding: Chamber relative humidity shall be less than 10%.
safety_implication: Controls moisture interference in low-temperature droplet combustion chemistry.
evidence: _Relative humidity:_ chamber relative humidity shall be less than 10%.
earth_application: Controlled laboratory combustion setups.

finding: Micro-gravity level accelerations are required to be less than 10^-5 m/s^2 in order to ensure buoyant forces are negligible.
safety_implication: Guarantees pure diffusive transport conditions matching theoretical spacecraft fire models.
evidence: _Micro-gravity levels:_ accelerations are required to be less than 10^(_−_5) _m/s_^2 in order to ensure buoyant forces are negligible.
earth_application: Buoyancy-free fundamental combustion testing.

finding: Droplet imaging requires a focal plane parallel to support fiber, FOV at least 3.0 cm centered on droplet, and 50 microm resolution.
safety_implication: Ensures optical diagnostics can accurately track droplet regression and burning phenomena for safety data collection.
evidence:
- focal plane parallel to support fiber
- FOV at least 3.0 _cm_ (5_._0_cm_, preferred) centered on droplet (center of FOV)
- resolution of 50_µm_ for smallest droplet size over entire FOV
earth_application: Optical diagnostics in spray combustion safety research.

finding: Flame radiation radiometers must be positioned at least 15 cm from the droplet to enable detection of all incident radiation with a response time constant less than 50 ms.
safety_implication: Reliable radiation sensing is essential for characterizing thermal hazards and heat feedback from spacecraft fires.
evidence:
- radiometers shall be positioned at least 15_cm_ from the droplet to enable detection of all incident radiation from the flame.
- response time constant to be _<_ 50_ms_
earth_application: Fire radiometry and heat flux sensor calibration.

finding: The droplet imaging system requires a minimum field of view of 3.0 cm centered about the droplet with 5.0 cm preferred, a resolution of 50 µm, and a minimum frame rate of 30 fps to accurately measure droplet size, burning rates, and extinction diameters.
safety_implication: Accurate droplet combustion characterization under microgravity ensures safe fuel handling and combustion system design for spacecraft.
evidence: Field of view: minimum of 3.0 cm centered about the droplet, 5.0 cm preferred Resolution: 50 µm over the entire FOV. Minimum frame rate: 30 fps over the duration of the test.
other_measurements: Field of view: 3.0 cm min, 5.0 cm preferred; Resolution: 50 µm; Frame rate: 30 fps
earth_application: Improves industrial droplet combustion efficiency and safety in liquid-fuel burners.

finding: Hot-flame imaging using UV OH-radical chemiluminescence or CH-radical emission requires a field of view of at least 8.0 cm (10.0 cm desired) and color filters targeting 310 nm or 430 nm at 30 fps to capture flame structure and dynamics.
safety_implication: Reliable hot-flame detection and monitoring protects crew and vehicle by tracking high-temperature combustion boundaries.
evidence: Field of view: minimum of 8.0 cm, 10.0 cm (desired) Depth of view: minimum 3.0 cm, 5.0 cm (desired) Color: shall detect wavelengths of 310 nm ± 5 nm or 430 nm ± 5 nm using an intensified camera in order to detect OH∗ or CH radical emission, respectively.
other_measurements: FOV: 8.0-10.0 cm; Wavelength: 310 nm or 430 nm; Frame rate: 30 fps
earth_application: Advances combustion diagnostic tools for high-temperature flames.

finding: Cool-flame imaging requires detecting excited formaldehyde (CH2O) chemiluminescence between approximately 390 nm and 490 nm using an intensified camera with sufficient sensitivity to detect weak cool-flame emissions near extinction.
safety_implication: Detecting hard-to-see cool flames prevents unmonitored secondary combustion hazards and uncontained reaction propagation in spacecraft environments.
evidence: Color: shall detect wavelengths between approximately 390 nm and 490 nm using an intensified camera in order to detect CH2O emission. Resolution: 100 µm (i.e. > 5 lp/mm) over the entire FOV. Minimum frame rate: 30 fps over the duration of the test.
other_measurements: Wavelength: 390-490 nm; Frame rate: 30 fps
earth_application: Improves detection limits for low-temperature oxidation and cool-flame hazards in chemical processing.

finding: Broadband and narrowband radiometers are required to measure total flame radiation between 0.6 µm and 5 µm and water vapor radiation between 6.0 µm and 6.5 µm with a sample rate of at least 20 Hz to establish the exact moment of hot and cool flame extinction.
safety_implication: Accurate extinction tracking prevents reignition risks and provides critical thermal data for vehicle fire protection systems.
evidence: Broad-band spectrum: radiometer used for broad-band radiation shall detect wavelengths within a band from 0.6 µm − 5 µm. Sample rate: data sampled from the radiometer shall be at a frequency of at least 20 Hz.
other_measurements: Sample rate: 20 Hz; Bandwidth: 0.6-5 µm
earth_application: Enhances fire detection sensitivity and thermal radiation monitoring in industrial burners.

finding: Ambient chamber temperature and pressure measurements require a minimum sample rate of 10 Hz, with temperature accuracy of at least ±0.5 C in the range of 18-27 C and pressure accuracy of ±0.01 atm in the range of 0.5-5.0 atm.
safety_implication: Precise monitoring of ambient conditions ensures test parameters remain within safety limits and validates environmental controls in spacecraft habitats.
evidence: Ambient Pressure and Temperature Measurement - minimum sample rate shall be at 10 Hz - temperature accuracy shall be at least ± 0.5 C in the range of 18 − 27 C - pressure accuracy shall be at least ± 0.01 atm in the range of 0.5 − 3 atm.
other_measurements: Temperature accuracy: ± 0.5 C; Pressure accuracy: ± 0.01 atm; Sample rate: 10 Hz
earth_application: Enables strict environmental control and monitoring in high-pressure combustion test facilities.

finding: All experimental measurements must be time-synchronized to GMT with a minimum accuracy of ±0.03 sec to enable accurate evaluation of droplet regression rate, flame structure, and flame extinction.
safety_implication: Reliable time synchronization is crucial for post-test failure analysis and reconstructing accidental fire timelines during space missions.
evidence: Time synchronization: all measurements shall be referenced to GMT with a minimum accuracy of ± 0.03 sec.
other_measurements: Time accuracy: ± 0.03 sec
earth_application: Ensures precise data correlation in multi-sensor industrial testing systems.

finding: The nominal test matrix for n-dodecane droplets ranging from 2 to 6 mm specifies nitrogen, helium, and xenon diluents across a range of oxygen mole fractions and pressures up to 5 atm.
safety_implication: Establishes baseline envelope conditions for droplet combustion and extinction limits in spacecraft environments.
evidence: Table 3: Nominal test matrix for n-dodecane. The droplet size range for the tests is 2 - 6 mm.
variables: Pressure, oxygen mole fraction, diluent type
partial_g_applicability: Applicable to spacecraft fire safety design under microgravity conditions.
earth_application: Improves foundational understanding of droplet combustion safety and fire suppression in liquid fuel systems.

finding: The nominal test matrix for additional fuels and fuel mixtures (such as n-dodecane/iso-octane, n-dodecane/2,6,10 trimethyldodecane, decane/2,2,4,6,6 pentamethylheptane, octane/n-propyl benzene/1,3,5 trimethyl benzene, and octane/2,2,4 trimethylpentane mixtures) covers nitrogen diluents over oxygen mole fractions and pressures up to 5 atm.
safety_implication: Provides crucial flammability limits and extinction boundaries for alternative hydrocarbon fuel blends relevant to space exploration logistics.
evidence: Table 4: Nominal test matrix for the other fuels and fuel mixtures. The droplet size range for the tests is 2 - 6 mm.
fuel_material: Various fuel mixtures including n-dodecane, iso-octane, n-heptane, 2,6,10 trimethyldodecane, decane, pentamethylheptane, octane, n-propyl benzene, 1,3,5 trimethyl benzene, and trimethylpentane
variables: Fuel composition, pressure, oxygen mole fraction
partial_g_applicability: Applicable to spacecraft fuel storage and fire hazards in microgravity.
earth_application: Aids in assessing fire hazards of complex multi-component liquid fuel mixtures in industrial applications.

finding: The Saffire experiments evaluate large-scale flame spread and growth on flammable material approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide.
safety_implication: Understanding large-scale flame spread on spacecraft materials ensures crew safety and proper material selection for future exploration vehicles.
evidence: The first objective is to understand the flame spread and growth of a fire over a large piece of flammable material, consistent with clothing or other fabric likely to be in a spacecraft cabin. This sample material is approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide.
earth_application: Improves material flammability safety standards and large-scale fire propagation models for terrestrial applications.

finding: Saffire-I uses a composite fabric sample consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass by weight (SIBAL cloth) and will be conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s.
safety_implication: Determines how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and whether it reaches a steady-state spread rate.
evidence: The sample material for Saffire-I and III is a composite fabric consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight)... Saffire-I will be conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s

finding: Saffire-III uses a composite fabric sample consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass by weight (SIBAL cloth) and will be run at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s.
safety_implication: Provides insight into large-scale fire growth and steady-state spread rates under varying airflow conditions in low gravity.
evidence: The sample material for Saffire-I and III is a composite fabric consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight)... Saffire-III will be run at a flow velocity of 30 cm/s .

finding: Saffire-II has a sample card containing 9 samples, each measuring 5 cm x 29 cm.
safety_implication: Enables multi-material flammability limit evaluation in low gravity to support spacecraft material selection.
evidence: Saffire-II has a sample card that contains 9 samples, each 5 cm x 29 cm.
fuel_material: Multiple sample materials including SIBAL, Silicone, PMMA, and Nomex

finding: Sample S1 consists of silicone with a thickness of 0.25 mm, tested with an air flow of 20 cm/s and an upstream igniter position.
safety_implication: Quantifies the flammability parameters of thin silicone under specific air flow conditions in microgravity.
evidence: S1 | Silicone | 0.25 mm | 20 | Upstream
earth_application: Understanding material flammability limits in different gravitational and flow environments.

finding: Sample S2 consists of silicone with a thickness of 0.61 mm, tested with an air flow of 20 cm/s and an upstream igniter position.
safety_implication: Evaluates the effect of increased thickness on silicone flammability in long-duration low-gravity.
evidence: S2 | Silicone | 0.61 mm | 20 | Upstream
earth_application: Material safety selection based on thickness.

finding: Sample S3 consists of silicone with a thickness of 1.02 mm, tested with an air flow of 20 cm/s and an upstream igniter position.
safety_implication: Assesses thicker silicone samples for flammability limits in microgravity.
evidence: S3 | Silicone | 1.02 mm | 20 | Upstream
earth_application: Spacecraft material flammability mitigation.

finding: Sample S4 consists of silicone with a thickness of 0.36 mm, tested with an air flow of 20 cm/s and a downstream igniter position.
safety_implication: Tests the effect of downstream ignition on silicone flammability.
evidence: S4 | Silicone | 0.36 mm | 20 | Downstream
earth_application: Understanding ignition source location effects on flame spread.

finding: Sample S5 consists of SIBAL fabric with a thickness of 0.33 mm, tested with an air flow of 20 cm/s and an upstream igniter position.
safety_implication: Evaluates fabric flammability limits under low airflow in microgravity.
evidence: S5 | SIBAL fabric | 0.33 mm | 20 | Upstream
earth_application: Textile and fabric fire safety standards.

finding: Sample S6 consists of SIBAL fabric with a thickness of 0.33 mm, tested with an air flow of 30 cm/s and an upstream igniter position.
safety_implication: Tests the effect of higher airflow velocity on SIBAL fabric flammability.
evidence: S6 | SIBAL fabric | 0.33 mm | 30 | Upstream
earth_application: Optimizing ventilation safety parameters in confined habitats.

finding: Sample S7 consists of PMMA to Nomex transition with a thickness of 0.33 mm, tested with an air flow of 20 cm/s and an upstream igniter position.
safety_implication: Measures flame propagation across material boundaries (PMMA to Nomex) in microgravity.
evidence: S7 | PMMA to Nomex | 0.33 mm | 20 | Upstream
earth_application: Understanding fire barrier effectiveness and multi-material interactions.

finding: Sample S8 consists of structured PMMA with a 10 mm thickness (with tapered edge for ignition), tested with an air flow of 20 cm/s and an upstream igniter position.
safety_implication: Evaluates thick structured combustible polymers under microgravity airflow conditions.
evidence: S8 | Structured PMMA | 10 mm (with tapered edge for ignition) | 20 | Upstream
earth_application: Fire safety assessment of thick structural plastics in buildings or vehicles.

finding: Sample S9 consists of flat PMMA with a 10 mm thickness (with tapered edge for ignition), tested with an air flow of 30 cm/s and an upstream igniter position.
safety_implication: Examines thick flat PMMA flammability at higher flow velocity in low-gravity environments.
evidence: S9 | Flat PMMA | 10 mm (with tapered edge for ignition) | 30 | Upstream
earth_application: Evaluating thick combustible structural elements under forced airflow.

finding: Drop tower testing has demonstrated that the flammability limits (MOC) of a material can be different in low-g than in normal gravity.
safety_implication: Standard 1-g flammability testing (like NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) may not accurately predict material behavior in long-duration spaceflight, risking spacecraft safety.
evidence: Drop tower testing has demonstrated the MOC flammability limits of a material can be different in low-g than in normal gravity [3-5].
earth_application: Understanding gravity-induced buoyancy effects on flammability limits.

finding: The Saffire-II experiment aims to quantify flammability limits using large samples of the same size as those used in NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 normal-gravity tests.
safety_implication: Provides direct comparison data between standard ground tests and long-duration space flight conditions to ensure crew and vehicle safety.
evidence: Therefore, the objective of the Saffire-II tests is to quantify that affect in long-duration low-gravity using samples of the same size as those used in the in NASASTD-6001 Test 1 normal-gravity tests [3].
earth_application: Improvement of standard flammability test protocols.

finding: Flow temperature is measured using thermocouples located at the inlet and outlet of the flow duct.
safety_implication: Enables thermal monitoring of the experiment environment to track fire progression and heat distribution.
evidence: Flow temperature | thermocouples | inlet and outlet of flow duct
earth_application: Duct fire and HVAC monitoring safety systems.

finding: Flame temperature is measured using thermocouples embedded in the sample.
safety_implication: Provides direct measurement of burning temperature within the solid fuel.
evidence: Flame temperature | thermocouples | embedded in sample
earth_application: Material thermal degradation and combustion research.

finding: Plume temperature is measured using a thermocouple.
safety_implication: Tracks hot gas plume dynamics exiting the combustion zone.
evidence: Plume temperature | thermoocouple |
earth_application: Fire plume tracking in confined environments.

finding: Flame radiation is measured using four radiometers, with two viewing the front of the sample and two viewing the back.
safety_implication: Quantifies radiative heat transfer from the flame to evaluate thermal hazards to surrounding spacecraft structures.
evidence: Flame radiation | radiometers | two viewing front of sample; two viewing back of sample
earth_application: Radiative heat transfer analysis in industrial fires.

finding: CO2 mole fraction is measured using a solid-state sensor located in the avionics bay.
safety_implication: Monitors combustion product generation and cabin air quality degradation during a fire event.
evidence: CO2mole fraction | solid‐state sensor | in avionics bay
earth_application: Indoor air quality and fire combustion gas monitoring.

finding: O2 mole fraction is measured using a solid-state sensor located at the inlet to the avionics bay.
safety_implication: Tracks oxygen consumption during combustion to determine extinction limits and habitat life support safety.
evidence: O2mole fraction | solid‐state sensor | inlet to avionics bay
earth_application: Oxygen depletion monitoring in enclosed spaces.

finding: Pressure is measured using a solid-state sensor located in the avionics bay.
safety_implication: Monitors pressure changes associated with combustion or system operations in a sealed spacecraft environment.
evidence: Pressure | solid‐state sensor | in avionics bay
earth_application: Pressure containment safety in closed vessels.

finding: Flow velocity is measured using two anemometers, with one placed on each side of the sample.
safety_implication: Ensures accurate ventilation velocity measurements across the burning fuel sample.
evidence: Flow velocity | anemometers | one on each side of sample
earth_application: Wind tunnel and HVAC airflow monitoring.

finding: Flame images are captured using two cameras viewing the front of the sample card as primary data measurements.
safety_implication: Provides visual documentation of flame spread rate, shape, and extinction behavior.
evidence: Flame image | cameras | two viewing front of sample
earth_application: Optical fire detection and monitoring.

finding: Flow uniformity is verified using a smoke wire located at the leading edge of the sample.
safety_implication: Verifies smooth and uniform airflow delivery to the combustion experiment.
evidence: Flow uniformity | smoke wire | leading edge of sample
earth_application: Flow visualization in aerodynamic testing.

finding: The Saffire-I flight unit was successfully launched within the Cygnus PCM on an Atlas V launch vehicle on March 22, 2016 as part of the OA-6 mission.
safety_implication: Ensures flight hardware survives launch environments and reaches the designated operational orbit safely.
evidence: The Saffire-I flight unit was successfully launched within the Cygnus PCM on an Atlas V launch vehicle on March 22, 2016 as part of the OA-6 mission.

finding: Inadvertent igniter activation prior to Cygnus deberthing from the ISS is identified as a major safety hazard resulting in the exposure of the flight crew to toxic gases produced by the combustion event.
safety_implication: Preventing premature ignition protects the ISS crew from toxic combustion gases when the Cygnus hatch is opened.
evidence: The major safety hazard is inadvertent igniter activation prior to the Cygnus deberthing from the ISS. This would result in the exposure of the flight crew to toxic gases that are produced from the combustion event.
earth_application: Prevents accidental ignition and toxic gas exposure in sealed industrial or aerospace environments.

finding: Four latching relays controlled and monitored by Cygnus avionics are used to control the hazard of inadvertent ignition, requiring a separate ground command to close each relay.
safety_implication: Multiple redundant electrical interlocks ensure that accidental activation of the igniter cannot occur without explicit multi-step ground commanding.
evidence: There are two latching relays in each of these two power feed circuits, one in the power feed side, one in the return. These four latching relays are contained within the Saffire flight unit but are controlled and monitored by Cygnus avionics. A separate ground command to the Cygnus avionics is required to close each of these four latching relays.
earth_application: Implements multi-failure tolerant electrical safety interlocks for high-hazard remote systems.

finding: Saffire-I, II, and III quantify the growth and end state of realistic fires in spacecraft and their influence on vehicle habitability to validate computational models.
safety_implication: Validation of computational models helps ensure crew safety and vehicle habitability during deep space exploration missions.
evidence: Quantify growth and end state of realistic fires in spacecraft and their influence on vehicle habitability
partial_g_applicability: Applicable to micro-g and exploration spacecraft environments.
earth_application: Improves compartment fire modeling and safety assessments for terrestrial enclosures.

finding: Saffire-IV, V, and VI evaluate flame behavior in complex geometries representing more realistic configurations than earlier Saffire tests.
safety_implication: Understanding flame spread over complex geometries improves fire safety assessments in realistic spacecraft cabin layouts.
evidence: Flame behavior in complex geometries
partial_g_applicability: Directly supports spacecraft fire safety design.
earth_application: Aids in evaluating complex geometry fire spread in terrestrial buildings and vehicles.

finding: Saffire-IV, V, and VI study flame behavior for planar and complex geometries in exploration atmospheres featuring elevated O2 and lower pressure.
safety_implication: Exploration atmospheres with elevated oxygen and reduced pressure pose severe flammability risks that must be quantified for crew protection.
evidence: Flame behavior for planar and complex geometries in exploration atmospheres
partial_g_applicability: Relevant to spacecraft and habitat exploration atmospheres.
earth_application: Applicable to hyperbaric or oxygen-enriched industrial or medical environments on Earth.

finding: Saffire-I and III measure flame behavior over large-scale planar surfaces.
safety_implication: Large-scale flame spread data ensures accurate prediction of fire propagation on spacecraft panels and structural materials.
evidence: Measure flame behavior over large-scale planar surfaces
partial_g_applicability: Validates spacecraft material safety.
earth_application: Improves large-scale material flammability tests for building materials.

finding: Saffire-IV, V, and VI demonstrate the performance of prototype Orion and ISS combustion product monitors.
safety_implication: Reliable post-fire monitoring ensures that combustion products are properly detected and tracked to protect astronaut health.
evidence: Demonstrate performance of prototype Orion and ISS combustion product monitor
sensors: prototype Orion and ISS combustion product monitor
partial_g_applicability: Essential for Orion and ISS safety systems.
earth_application: Enhances toxic gas monitoring systems in enclosed environments on Earth.

finding: Saffire-IV, V, and VI obtain data to validate transport and detection models required for model development.
safety_implication: Validating transport and detection models allows accurate placement and response calibration of smoke and gas detectors.
evidence: Obtain data to validate transport and detection models
partial_g_applicability: Critical for dependable early warning detection in spacecraft.
earth_application: Improves smoke and gas transport modeling in residential and commercial buildings.

finding: Saffire-IV, V, and VI quantify the rate of decay of gas species after a spacecraft fire.
safety_implication: Knowing post-fire gas species decay rates dictates when crew members can safely remove respirators or re-enter a module.
evidence: Quantify rate of decay of gas species after a spacecraft fire
partial_g_applicability: Directly impacts spacecraft post-fire recovery procedures.
earth_application: Aids toxicological risk assessment following industrial and structural fires.

finding: Saffire-IV, V, and VI quantify atmosphere cleanup rate with a prototype smoke-eater.
safety_implication: Demonstrating prototype smoke-eater hardware ensures effective scrubbing of harmful particulates and gases from spacecraft cabin air.
evidence: Quantify atmosphere cleanup rate with prototype smoke-eater
partial_g_applicability: Essential for restoring cabin habitability on long-duration exploration missions.
earth_application: Improves air purification technologies for smoke removal after fires.

finding: ACME investigates laminar, gaseous, non-premixed flames in microgravity to improve terrestrial combustion efficiency and reduce pollutant emissions.
safety_implication: Improving fundamental combustion models helps refine terrestrial combustion applications and supports spacecraft fire safety assessments.
evidence: ACME is focused on advanced combustion technology via fundamental microgravity research. The primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion. A secondary objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft.
earth_application: Improving efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions in practical terrestrial combustion.

finding: An ACME precursor, the Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE), was conducted in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) in early 2012.
safety_implication: Precursor experiments like SLICE build foundational data for subsequent flight projects like ACME.
evidence: An ACME precursor, Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE), was conducted in the ISS’ Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) in early 2012.

finding: ACME includes independent experiments investigating laminar, gaseous, non-premixed flames where the fuel is a gas and fuel and oxygen are on opposite sides of the flame sheet.
safety_implication: Understanding non-premixed flame behavior supports fundamental combustion research and safety hazard mitigation.
evidence: The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project includes six independent experiments investigating laminar gaseous non-premixed flames. In other words, the flow is smooth and without vortices, the fuel is a gas (and not a liquid or solid), and the fuel and oxygen are not mixed in the burner (but are instead on opposite sides of the flame sheet).
earth_application: Terrestrial combustor design and pollutant reduction.

finding: ACME research targets fuel-lean combustion conditions, soot control, oxygen-enriched combustion, flame stability and extinction limits, and electric fields for combustion control.
safety_implication: Expands knowledge of extinction limits and flame stability to improve spacecraft fire prevention and material screening tests.
evidence: Some specific ACME goals are to improve our understanding of combustion at fuel lean conditions where both optimum performance and low emissions can be achieved, soot control and reduction, oxygen-enriched combustion which could enable practical carbon sequestration, flame stability and extinction limits, and the use of electric fields for combustion control.
earth_application: Optimizing industrial combustion and carbon sequestration.

finding: ACME spacecraft fire prevention research aims to understand materials flammability, extinction behavior, and sustained combustion conditions to assess existing flammability test methods.
safety_implication: Enhances crew safety by ensuring spacecraft materials are accurately screened and selected using robust flammability criteria.
evidence: The goal of ACME’s spacecraft fire prevention research is to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability test methods for the screening and selection of materials for spacecraft.
earth_application: Material flammability testing standards.

finding: The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) focuses on fire prevention in spacecraft by improving fundamental understanding of material flammability, including ignition and extinction behavior, and assessing existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.
safety_implication: Improving flammability assessments and understanding ignition and extinction under low and partial-gravity directly supports spacecraft fire prevention and materials selection for Moon and Mars missions.
evidence: Specifically, BRE’s objective is to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as ignition and extinction behavior, and assess the relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.
fuel_material: gaseous fuel simulating paper, plastic, and alcohol
variables: fuel flow rate based on measured heat flux and surface temperature
partial_g_applicability: Assesses flammability test methods specifically for low and partial-gravity environments.
earth_application: Enhances fundamental understanding of material flammability and test methods relevant to terrestrial fire safety.

finding: Current predictive capability for flames at extremes of fuel dilution, such as sooty pure-fuel flames and near-extinction dilute flames, is significantly lacking in microgravity.
safety_implication: Identifying gaps in flame prediction capabilities near extinction helps avoid unexpected fire growth or failure to predict combustion hazards in spacecraft environments.
evidence: Research, especially including that already conducted in microgravity, has revealed that our current predictive ability is significantly lacking for flames at the extremes of fuel dilution, namely for sooty purefuel flames and dilute flames that are near extinction.
earth_application: Improves general combustion modeling for extreme fuel dilution and soot formation in terrestrial combustion systems.

finding: Sooty microgravity flames are wider, taller, cooler, and nearly a factor of ten higher in soot concentration compared to their normal gravity counterparts due to the absence of buoyancy.
safety_implication: Understanding that microgravity flames exhibit significantly higher soot concentrations helps in designing effective smoke and soot detection systems as well as predicting combustion hazards in spacecraft.
evidence: Sooty microgravity flames are wider and taller than their normal gravity counterparts, and the concentration of soot can be larger by nearly a factor of ten.
other_measurements: soot concentration larger by nearly a factor of ten
earth_application: Improves computer models of soot formation and destruction, benefiting combustion technology and environmental health on Earth.

finding: Highly diluted fuels with inert gas (nitrogen) can produce stable flames in microgravity that would not be possible under normal gravity conditions.
safety_implication: Knowledge of weak, highly diluted flame limits and stabilization mechanisms in microgravity is critical for spacecraft fire safety and defining spacecraft flammability limits.
evidence: microgravity flames are seen to behave quite differently, with highly diluted fuels producing stable flames that would not be possible under normal gravity conditions.
fuel_material: methane and ethylene diluted with nitrogen
earth_application: Important for understanding stabilization mechanisms and dilution limits for practical combustion systems on Earth.

finding: For sooty flames, the absence of gravity results in flames that are taller, wider, cooler, and far sootier compared to normal gravity.
safety_implication: Demonstrates that combustion behavior scales drastically in microgravity, impacting fire detection and suppression strategies for space exploration vehicles.
evidence: Flames are taller, wider, cooler, and far sootier in microgravity as compared to normal gravity.
earth_application: Enhances fundamental understanding of gravity effects on soot production.

finding: Microgravity flames contain five to eight times more soot than equivalent normal gravity flames as indicated by soot volume fraction measurements.
safety_implication: Increased soot production in spacecraft microgravity environments significantly raises the risk of cabin contamination and optical sensor obstruction compared to Earth-based combustion.
evidence: Soot volume fraction measurements indicate that microgravity flames contain five to eight times more soot than the equivalent normal gravity flames.

finding: Highly diluted weak flames exhibit greater stability in microgravity than in normal gravity, with extended dilution limits enabling lifted flames at lower fuel concentrations.
safety_implication: The ability of lean or heavily diluted fires to remain stable and persist at lower fuel concentrations in microgravity poses unexpected persistence and detection challenges for spacecraft safety systems.
evidence: The data has shown that for highly diluted weak flames, microgravity flames are more stable than their normal gravity counterparts. The dilution limits are extended allowing for lifted flames at lower fuel concentrations than observed in normal gravity.

finding: Electric fields influence flames through ion transport and induced ion winds, which can modify flame shape, alter soot or flammability limits, direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutant emissions.
safety_implication: Using electric fields to control ion transport can potentially serve as an active suppression or fire control mechanism in spacecraft environments where traditional buoyancy-driven flows are absent.
evidence: Electric fields can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions present as a result of the combustion reactions. The direct ion transport and the induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot or flammability limits, direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutant emission.
earth_application: Electric fields can be utilized to reduce pollutant emissions and control combustion processes in terrestrial burners and industrial applications.

finding: Electric field experiments will use a normal coflow flame or simple gas-jet flame with high voltage differentials up to 10 kV between the burner and a flat circular mesh downstream to measure ion current and response time.
safety_implication: Understanding combustion behavior under electric fields helps improve fundamental knowledge of combustion processes for spacecraft safety.
evidence: The experiment will be conducted with a normal coflow flame (as in the CLD Flame experiment) or perhaps with a simple gas-jet flame, where there is no surrounding coflow. An electric field will be generated by creating a high voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.
fuel_geometry: coflow flame or simple gas-jet flame
earth_application: Improves combustion processes and burner designs on Earth.

finding: The Flame Design experiment aims to improve understanding of soot inception and control to optimize oxygen enriched combustion and design robust, soot-free nonpremixed flames.
safety_implication: Soot reduction and better flame control prevent fire hazards and particulate accumulation in spacecraft cabin environments.
evidence: The primary goal of the Flame Design experiment is to improve our understanding of soot inception and control in order to enable the optimization of oxygen enriched combustion and the “design” of nonpremixed flames that are both robust and soot free.
variables: concentrations of injected fuel and oxygen enriched atmosphere
earth_application: Enables efficient and less polluting burner designs on Earth.

finding: Flame Design will investigate soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames using ethylene or methane in oxygen enriched atmospheres.
safety_implication: Identifying soot inception and extinction limits aids in preventing hazardous carbonaceous deposits and unexpected flame extinction during spacecraft operations.
evidence: Flame Design will investigate the soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames, created in the same manner as for the s-Flame experiment. Tests will be conducted with various concentrations of both the injected fuel (i.e., ethylene or methane) and the oxygen enriched atmosphere in order to determine the role of the flame structure on soot inception.
variables: concentrations of injected fuel and oxygen enriched atmosphere
earth_application: Optimization of oxygen-enriched combustion processes.

finding: The Flame Design experiment explores whether the stoichiometric mixture fraction can characterize soot and flammability limits for non-premixed flames.
safety_implication: Understanding flammability limits and soot formation mechanisms helps improve spacecraft fire safety and material selection criteria.
evidence: The Flame Design experiment will explore whether the stoichiometric mixture fraction can characterize soot and flammability limits for non-premixed flames like the equivalence ratio serves as an indicator of those limits for premixed flames.
fuel_geometry: Central tube and surrounding annulus injection

finding: Spherical diffusion flames are created using a porous spherical burner in microgravity to investigate structure, dynamics, and extinction limits.
safety_implication: Predicting flame extinction and instability limits under microgravity conditions supports reliable spacecraft fire detection and suppression strategies.
evidence: The spherical flame, which is only possible in microgravity, will be created through use of a porous spherical burner from which a fuel/inert gas mixture will issue into the CIR chamber.
variables: inert diluents, fuel types (hydrogen, methane, ethylene)
earth_application: Improves fundamental combustion models used for engine and burner safety design.

finding: Quasi-steady spherical cool diffusion flames are studied using porous burners to understand combustion physics and thermal transport processes.
safety_implication: Cool flame chemistry impacts ignition and flame propagation, which is vital for preventing unexpected fires and optimizing fire suppression systems in spacecraft habitats.
evidence: A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this research.
earth_application: Relevant to internal combustion engines and fuel octane/cetane number determination.

finding: Flicker, a buoyancy-driven instability, is eliminated in microgravity, yielding quasisteady flames.
safety_implication: Understanding flame stability without buoyancy-driven flicker helps model spacecraft fires more accurately.
evidence: Flicker, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasisteady flames.

finding: Microgravity flames exhibit increased length scales which facilitate the analysis of flame structure.
safety_implication: Enables detailed spatial tracking of flame zones for fire detection and prevention sensor design.
evidence: Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.

finding: Momentum-dominated flames can be studied at low velocities in microgravity to simplify analysis.
safety_implication: Aids in understanding forced-flow ventilation effects on spacecraft fire propagation.
evidence: Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.

finding: Microgravity flames show a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and a broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames due to near absence of buoyant entrainment.
safety_implication: Spacecraft atmosphere composition changes can drastically alter material flammability.
evidence: Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.

finding: Long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, although many microgravity flames are soot-free.
safety_implication: Informs smoke and particulate detector sensitivity requirements for spacecraft cabins.
evidence: The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.

finding: Soot, extinction, and stability limits are investigated in ACME experiments.
safety_implication: Establishing extinction and stability boundaries ensures spacecraft fire extinguishment strategies are effective.
evidence: Microgravity flames are great for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. Soot, extinction, and stability limits are being studied in the ACME experiments.

finding: ACME equipment includes surface thermocouples on most burners and two heat flux transducers on each burner dedicated to the BRE experiment.
safety_implication: Monitoring temperatures and heat fluxes provides critical thermal tracking to prevent equipment over-heating and unauthorized fire growth inside the spacecraft facility.
evidence: Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each burner for the BRE experiment will have two heat flux transducers.
partial_g_applicability: Applies to microgravity combustion facilities on space vehicles.
earth_application: Laboratory burner thermal management and heat flux characterization.

finding: Porous burner internal pressures are measured to monitor the differential pressure across the outlet surface.
safety_implication: Monitoring internal burner pressure ensures stable fuel and gas delivery and prevents flashback or backpressure anomalies.
evidence: The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface.
partial_g_applicability: Relevant to closed-chamber spaceflight combustion operations.
earth_application: Porous burner safety and flow integrity monitoring.

finding: ACME uses smaller standard bottle sizes (1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters) as a hazard control to limit the amount of deficient reactant like fuel that can be released into the combustion chamber.
safety_implication: Restricting reactant bottle volumes is a critical engineering hazard control to minimize the risk of unignited fuel accumulation and subsequent deflagration inside the spacecraft.
evidence: CIR’s standard bottle sizes are 1, 2.25, and 3.8 liters but ACME will sometimes use smaller bottles as a hazard control to limit the deficient reactant (e.g., fuel) that can be released into the combustion chamber.
partial_g_applicability: Critical for spacecraft safety where total volume and atmosphere venting are strictly constrained.
earth_application: Hazard control and storage volume limitation for flammable gases in industrial settings.

finding: ACME primary flame diagnostics include a suite of imaging systems comprising five video cameras and two illumination systems.
safety_implication: Enables comprehensive optical monitoring and diagnostics of combustion behavior for spacecraft fire safety hardware design.
evidence: ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and two illumination systems.
earth_application: Improves combustion imaging techniques used in terrestrial laboratory burners.

finding: The imaging systems enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging, pyrometry, soot volume fraction measurement, and operational support.
safety_implication: Detailed optical data allows tracking of soot and radical formation, key indicators of combustion hazards in microgravity.
evidence: Collectively, the imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot volume fraction; and/or operational support.
sensors: CH* camera, OH* camera, pyrometer, soot volume fraction measurement system
earth_application: Advances soot and radical emission measurement techniques in industrial combustion systems.

finding: Color imaging is provided by a high-definition digital camera mounted outside the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert.
safety_implication: Dual camera configuration ensures robust visual feedback for monitoring combustion experiments and flame structure.
evidence: Color imaging is provided by two video cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning mirror).
sensors: high-definition digital camera, standard analog camera
earth_application: Improves multi-angle visual monitoring in combustion test rigs.

finding: The analog camera signal is downlinked in near real time to support experiment operations, with LEDs used to illuminate the igniter and burner.
safety_implication: Real-time visual monitoring aids crew and ground operators in tracking ignition and burner status, preventing off-nominal combustion events.
evidence: The signal from the analog camera (shown below) will be downlinked in near real time to support the experiment operations, where Light-Emitting Diodes (LEDs) within the chamber can be used to illuminate the igniter and burner to both support the operations and provide reference images.
earth_application: Enhances remote monitoring and control capabilities for hazardous industrial combustion facilities.

finding: A 12-bit digital camera recording at up to 30 full frames per second with a resolution of 1360 by 1024 pixels and a motorized lens was used.
safety_implication: Enables precise optical diagnostic capabilities for combustion experiments in spaceflight missions.
evidence: The 12-bit digital camera (shown below) records at up to 30 full frames (1360×1024) per second, and is equipped with a motorized lens with independent control of the zoom, iris, and focus.
earth_application: Useful for combustion diagnostics and soot measurement in terrestrial laboratory flames.

finding: A filter assembly with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter is used for color-ratio pyrometry and soot volume fraction measurement while balancing color planes.
safety_implication: Allows accurate optical measurement of soot and temperature fields during spacecraft fire safety and combustion investigations.
evidence: Color imaging can also be carried out with a blue-green BG7 Schott glass filter, which balances the color planes to avoid saturation in the red while maintaining sensitivity in the blue and green. The natural flame color can be approximately reconstructed, but the primary purpose of the filter is color-ratio pyrometry and measurement of the soot volume fraction.
sensors: digital camera with BG7 Schott glass filter
earth_application: Improves optical diagnostic accuracy for soot and temperature in combustion research on Earth.

finding: CH* imaging is conducted using a 430-nm bandpass filter with a 10-nm FWHM, while a 450-nm bandpass filter with a 10-nm FWHM is used to subtract interfering broadband soot emission.
safety_implication: Enables accurate optical diagnostics and characterization of flame structures and soot interference for spacecraft fire detection and combustion safety research.
evidence: Alternately, CH* imaging can be conducted with this camera because the filter assembly includes a 430-nm bandpass filter with a 10-nm full width at half-maximum transmission (FWHM). A 450nm bandpass filter (again with a 10-nm FWHM) can be used with the CH* filter to effectively subtract interfering broadband soot emission.
sensors: CIR Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) package, 430-nm bandpass filter, 450-nm bandpass filter
earth_application: Improves optical diagnostic techniques for combustion research and soot detection systems in terrestrial laboratories.

finding: OH* is an excited radical molecule that emits ultraviolet light at 310 nm via chemiluminescence when dropping to a lower energy state.
safety_implication: Understanding UV emissions from radical species improves space-based fire detection and flame monitoring capabilities.
evidence: OH* is an excited (radical) molecule that emits light at 310 nm, which is in the ultraviolet, when it drops to a lower energy state in a process known as chemiluminescence.
earth_application: Advances foundational understanding of radical chemistry and optical emission for terrestrial fire safety sensors.

finding: ACME performs OH* imaging using the CIR Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) package, consisting of a monochrome intensified camera covering 280-700 nm paired with a 310-nm bandpass filter with a 10-nm FWHM.
safety_implication: Provides precise spatial and spectral tracking of reaction zones in microgravity combustion environments for enhanced spacecraft fire safety.
evidence: ACME will carry out OH* imaging using CIR’s Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) package, which is a monochrome camera with an intensifier (for 280-700 nm) and a 310-nm bandpass filter (with a 10-nm FWHM) for OH* imaging.
sensors: CIR Low-Light-Level Ultraviolet (LLL-UV) package, Monochrome intensified camera, 310-nm bandpass filter
earth_application: Improves ultraviolet optical diagnostic tools used in combustion and flame research laboratories on Earth.

finding: Binning is employed to record OH* images at 512x512 resolution and 30 fps to compensate for signal loss through a narrow bandpass filter.
safety_implication: Ensures proper image capture and combustion monitoring in microgravity experiments despite optical component signal limitations.
evidence: As a result of the signal loss through the narrow bandpass filter, binning is employed such that the OH* images are recorded at 512×512 and 30 fps.

finding: Color ratio pyrometry utilizes a ratio of emitted light at different wavelengths to determine flame temperature where soot is visibly glowing.
safety_implication: Enables accurate thermal monitoring of hydrocarbon flames during spacecraft combustion experiments.
evidence: Yellow indicates a higher temperature than red, but a ratio of the light emitted at different wavelengths (or wavelength ranges) can be used to determine the temperature, but only where the soot is visibly glowing.

finding: Pyrometry can be performed using a monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral camera with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter, requiring a quasi-steady flame.
safety_implication: Requires stable combustion conditions to reliably measure spectral emissions in spaceflight hardware.
evidence: Pyrometry can be accomplished with CIR’s monochrome High-Bit Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, when equipped with a Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter (LCTF) for imaging at multiple spectra. However, it requires a quasi-steady flame for measurement at each desired wavelength band.
sensors: High-Bit Depth Multispectral camera, Liquid-Crystal Tunable Filter

finding: The HiBMs camera uses a telecentric optical system operating at 512x512 pixels and 30 fps due to binning necessitated by LCTF filter signal loss.
safety_implication: Compensates for optical signal loss to maintain reliable diagnostic imaging capabilities.
evidence: The HiBMs camera has a telecentric optical system and is recorded at 512×512 and 30 frames per second (fps). Although it has a 1024×1024 pixel array, binning has been necessary because of signal loss through the LCTF filter.

finding: Thin Filament Pyrometry using ceramic fibers can determine temperature in soot-free flames.
safety_implication: Provides a reliable temperature measurement method for non-sooting combustion environments where standard pyrometry fails.
evidence: For soot-free flames, Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) can be used to determine the flame temperature. Ceramic fibers are stretched across the flame and glow when hot, just like the soot particles.

finding: The ACME chamber insert features a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide fibers positioned orthogonally to the flame axis for TFP measurements.
safety_implication: Allows crew members to adjust and replace sensor elements to maintain experiment diagnostics safely.
evidence: ACME’s chamber insert is equipped with a crew-replaceable array of 5 silicon carbide (SiC) fibers. The TFP fibers are orthogonal to the flame axis and the array can be translated along the flame axis to the desired position downstream of the burner, e.g., based on the downlink of the analog video.

finding: During setup, the crew can manually orient the TFP fiber array orthogonally to either the HiBMs camera with LCTF or ACME's digital color camera.
safety_implication: Provides crew flexibility in configuring optical diagnostics for optimal data collection.
evidence: During set up, the crew can manually orient the TFP fiber array so that it is orthogonal to either the HiBMs camera with the LCTF or ACME’s digital color camera.

finding: Six far-field thermocouples can be accommodated by the ACME chamber insert to measure thermal field spread in spherical flame experiments.
safety_implication: Supports comprehensive thermal mapping of spherical flames to understand fire growth hazards in spacecraft environments.
evidence: As a supplement to the pyrometry, the ACME chamber insert can accommodate six far-field thermocouples to measure the spread of the thermal field in the spherical flame experiments.

finding: Thermocouples are positioned upstream of the burner tip and have limited utility for non-spherical experiments, and may be omitted by the crew to prevent accidental damage.
safety_implication: Prevents unnecessary hardware installation and lowers the risk of equipment damage during specific combustion configurations.
evidence: The thermocouples are of limited utility for the other experiments because they are positioned upstream of the burner tip. Therefore, they will generally not be installed by the crew to reduce the chance of accidental damage.

finding: Two versions of a four-thermocouple rake are available to provide near and far temperature measurements without extending downstream of the burner tip to avoid optical interference.
safety_implication: Ensures temperature sensor arrays do not obstruct optical measurement equipment or compromise experimental data.
evidence: There will be two versions of a four-thermocouple rake to allow a choice of near and far measurements. Other arrays could be designed to support future experiments, but they cannot extend downstream of the burner tip without interfering with other (e.g., optical) measurements.

finding: The amount of soot particulate in a flame is determined using an extinction technique with a camera and a collimated light source placed at opposite windows.
safety_implication: Enables accurate quantification of soot production in spacecraft fire scenarios, supporting better hazard detection and air quality management.
evidence: The amount of soot particulate in a flame can be determined via an extinction technique, where the camera and the collimated light source are positioned at opposite windows.
other_measurements: resolution: 1024x1024 pixels; frame rate: 30 fps
sensors: High-Bit Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, camera, collimated light source
earth_application: Improves combustion efficiency and emission monitoring in terrestrial burners and industrial furnaces.

finding: Soot volume fraction can be determined directly from a digital color camera using an alternate Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array including a platinum wire.
safety_implication: Provides robust in-flight characterization of soot parameters to ensure crew protection against harmful combustion byproducts.
evidence: Alternatively, the soot volume fraction can be determined directly from the digital color camera, where an alternate Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array including a platinum wire will be used for inflight characterization for that measurement.
sensors: digital color camera, Thin Filament Pyrometry (TFP) fiber array
earth_application: Advanced diagnostics for combustion emissions and particulate matter research.

finding: The ACME chamber insert includes a crew-exchangeable linear array of radiometers configured with two versions for initial experiments.
safety_implication: Allows precise thermal radiation monitoring from combustion experiments to prevent spacecraft overheating hazards.
evidence: The ACME chamber insert includes a crew-exchangeable linear array of radiometers of which there are two versions supporting the initial set of experiments.
earth_application: Optimizes radiant heat capture and thermal safety design in industrial combustion chambers.

finding: An additional fixed, wide-view radiometer positioned downstream at 30 degrees from the chamber axis is used to support spherical flame experiments with quicker response times.
safety_implication: Provides enhanced and rapid detection capabilities for spherical flames in spacecraft fire safety monitoring.
evidence: An additional wide-view radiometer, that is fixed and not crew exchangeable, is positioned downstream of the burner and flame at 30o from the chamber axis. This detector is primarily intended to support the spherical flame experiments and will have a quicker response than the more sensitive detectors that will used in the linear arrays.

finding: ACME radiometers utilize thermopile detectors with a spectral range of 0.2-11 microns and fields of view established by selected apertures rather than lenses.
safety_implication: Ensures robust thermal radiation measurement capabilities for combustion products and flame emissions during microgravity operations.
evidence: ACME’s radiometers are more precisely thermopile detectors with a spectral range of nominally 0.2-11 micron and fields of view that are established by appropriately selected apertures (i.e., rather than lenses).

finding: The chamber insert is equipped with a set of three Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules to detect the quenching of dim flames.
safety_implication: Enables the detection of near-extinction or dim flame behaviors critical for understanding fire suppression and preventing unburned fuel hazards.
evidence: To detect the quenching of dim flames, the chamber insert will be equipped with a set of three Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules.

finding: The ACME experiments are constant volume studies with a chamber free volume of about 90 liters, where tests typically last 0.5 to 2 minutes.
safety_implication: Understanding pressure rise and operational duration in a constant volume combustion chamber is critical for safe spacecraft fire safety design and preventing over-pressurization.
evidence: All ACME experiments will be constant volume (i.e., rather than constant pressure) studies, where the chamber’s free volume will be about 90 liters. Burner flows will generally be constrained to limit the pressure rise, and tests will typically be 0.5-2 minutes in duration.
other_measurements: chamber free volume: 90 liters; test duration: 0.5-2 minutes
earth_application: Applies to closed-vessel combustion safety and explosion hazard mitigation in industrial processes.

finding: BASS tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity with adequate ventilation burn as well or better than in normal gravity.
safety_implication: Understanding material flammability in microgravity is critical for spacecraft fire safety and prevention design.
evidence: Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) tests the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.).
earth_application: Contributes to combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems on Earth.

finding: For a microgravity fire, attacking the base of the flame as done on Earth may not be the optimal suppression strategy, and suppressant streams could potentially worsen the flame via oxygen entrainment.
safety_implication: Fire suppression protocols for spacecraft must account for modified flame behavior and geometry in micro-g to avoid worsening the fire.
evidence: For a fire burning in microgravity, the best point of application of suppressant may not be immediately apparent, especially for a partially obstructed flame or a wake-stabilized flame. Depending on the geometry of the flame and the characteristics of the extinguisher (distance from flame, dispersion angle) it is possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen.
earth_application: Improves general understanding of suppression mechanics involving obstructed or wake-stabilized flames.

finding: During BASS tests involving nitrogen suppressant systems, the nitrogen is engaged at a gradually increasing level until extinction of the flame is reached.
safety_implication: Understanding how nitrogen suppressant injection leads to extinction aids in developing effective fire suppression protocols and systems for spacecraft.
evidence: For many of these tests, the nitrogen suppressant system is engaged at a gradually increasing level until extinction is reached.
partial_g_applicability: Applicable to spacecraft fire safety where nitrogen or other inert gases are used for cabin fire suppression.
earth_application: Improves gaseous and inerting fire suppression systems used in enclosed environments on Earth.

finding: Important experimental observations for the burning process include flame shape and appearance as a function of flow speed, flame spread rate, and flame dynamics such as pulsations and oscillations.
safety_implication: Characterizing flame shape and spread dynamics helps predict fire growth rates under various ventilation conditions in microgravity habitats.
evidence: The important experimental observations from BASS with respect to the burning process include flame shape and appearance as a function of flow speed, flame spread rate (how fast the flame develops), and flame dynamics (pulsations, oscillations, etc.).
partial_g_applicability: Provides baseline understanding for partial-g fire growth models.
earth_application: Aids in understanding flame spread and dynamics in forced-flow environments on Earth, such as ventilation ducts.

finding: Critical extinction observations and data include the time to extinction as a function of fuel geometry, the nitrogen flow rate, and the flame distance from the nozzle.
safety_implication: Identifying extinction limits based on nitrogen flow rate and fuel geometry ensures reliable suppression sizing for spacecraft fire protection.
evidence: With respect to extinction, the critical observations and data are the time to extinction as a function of fuel geometry, the nitrogen flow rate, and the flame distance from the nozzle.
variables: fuel geometry, nitrogen flow rate, flame distance from nozzle
partial_g_applicability: Informs partial-g spacecraft suppression design.
earth_application: Improves design criteria for fire suppression systems in confined spaces.

finding: A zero-g facility test burned a 2-cm-diameter PMMA sphere in a 30 cm/s airflow, observing conditions at 1 g, 0 g at 1 s after drop, and 0 g at 4 s after application of a nitrogen extinguishing agent.
safety_implication: Demonstrates the transient response of a burning spherical fuel element when subjected to microgravity and subsequent nitrogen suppression.
evidence: Zero-g facility test burning 2-cm-diameter PMMA sphere in 30 cm/s airflow. Left: 1 g; Middle: 0 g, 1 s after drop; right: 0 g, 4 s after application of nitrogen extinguishing agent. PMMA Sphere
variables: gravity level, application of nitrogen extinguishing agent
partial_g_applicability: Relevant to spacecraft materials safety and spherical geometry combustion behaviors.
earth_application: Provides comparative data on spherical combustion and extinction between normal gravity and reduced gravity.

finding: Drop tower results and computer simulations captured the flame response of a 2-cm-diameter PMMA sphere burning in 17% oxygen at 1 atm pressure and 2 cm/s forced convective flow as it transitioned from 1-g to 0-g.
safety_implication: Validates computational models against drop tower experiments for predicting material flammability and flame behavior during gravity transitions.
evidence: Drop tower results and modeling of a 2-cm-diameter PMMA sphere burning in 17% oxygen, 1 atm. pressure, at 2 cm/s forced convective flow. Experiment images are overlaid with computer simulations, which can capture the flame response as it transitions from 1-g to 0-g.
partial_g_applicability: Assists in understanding how reduced gravity alters combustion limits and flame responses for spacecraft materials.
earth_application: Improves fundamental combustion models for spheres and validation techniques using drop towers.

finding: Forty-one test samples are burned across a variety of flow conditions yielding 89 test points.
safety_implication: Provides comprehensive combustion datasets across varied flow environments to improve spacecraft fire safety designs.
evidence: Forty-one test samples will be burned in a variety of flow conditions for a total of 89 test points.
other_measurements: test samples: 41; test points: 89

finding: Airflow rates through the BASS duct are adjusted by the crewmember from 5 to 50 cm/s.
safety_implication: Understanding flammability limits under specific low-speed flows helps determine spacecraft fire ignition thresholds.
evidence: The crewmember adjusts the airflow from 5 to 50 cm/s.

finding: Nitrogen suppressant is supplied via mass flow controller from 0 to 500 cc/min to extinguish the flame.
safety_implication: Evaluates the effectiveness of gaseous nitrogen suppression systems for spacecraft fire extinguishment.
evidence: A nitrogen suppressant is then supplied via a mass flow controller, from 0 to 500 cc/min.
other_measurements: nitrogen suppressant flow: 0 to 500 cc/min

finding: BASS-II utilizes slightly modified Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) hardware within the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) for observations of burning solid materials on board the ISS.
safety_implication: Using modified existing hardware on the ISS ensures experimental compatibility and safety while assessing solid material flammability.
evidence: Burning and Suppression of Solids – II (BASS-II) utilizes slightly modified Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) hardware within the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) for observations of burning solid materials on board the ISS.
fuel_material: acrylic films, acrylic sheets, cotton-fiberglass fabric blend SIBAL fuel, black or clear acrylic
fuel_geometry: flat samples, rod samples, and a section of a large solid sphere

finding: Thin flat samples (10 cm long by 1 and 2 cm wide) yield concurrent or opposed-flow spread rates, limiting flame lengths, and extinction limits.
safety_implication: Determining concurrent or opposed-flow spread rates and extinction limits for thin flat samples helps establish flammability boundaries for spacecraft materials.
evidence: Thin flat samples (10 cm long by 1 and 2 cm wide) yield concurrent or opposed-flow spread rates, limiting flame lengths, and extinction limits.
fuel_material: acrylic films, acrylic sheets, and SIBAL fuel
fuel_geometry: 10 cm long by 1 and 2 cm wide

finding: Rod samples made of black or clear acrylic provide solid fuel regression rates and extinction limits for both opposed and concurrent flow.
safety_implication: Solid fuel regression rates and extinction limits for rod samples assist in evaluating the flammability and burn-through potential of rod-shaped spacecraft components.
evidence: The rod samples are made of black or clear acrylic and will provide solid fuel regression rates and extinction limits for both opposed and concurrent flow.

finding: A large solid spherical section made of acrylic is used to study ignition of thick materials and flame growth over the thick material.
safety_implication: Studying the ignition and flame growth of thick materials is critical for assessing the fire hazards of thick structural components in spacecraft environments.
evidence: The large solid spherical section, also made of acrylic, will be used to study ignition of thick materials and flame growth over the thick material.

finding: Critical experimental observations regarding the burning process include flame shape and appearance as a function of ambient oxygen concentration, flow speed, flame spread rate, and flame dynamics such as pulsations and oscillations.
safety_implication: Understanding flame shape, spread rate, and dynamics under varying oxygen and flow conditions improves predictive fire growth models for crewed spacecraft.
evidence: The important experimental observations from BASS-II with respect to the burning process include flame shape and appearance as a function of ambient oxygen concentration, flow speed, flame spread rate (how fast the flame develops), and flame dynamics (pulsations, oscillations, etc.).

finding: Critical observations and data related to extinction include the time to extinction as a function of fuel geometry, flow, and ambient oxygen concentration.
safety_implication: Quantifying time to extinction under different environmental parameters provides essential data for fire suppression system design and post-ignition hazard assessment.
evidence: With respect to extinction, the critical observations and data are the time to extinction as a function of fuel geometry, flow, and ambient oxygen concentration.

finding: Theoretical models predict higher flame spread rates than those actually observed in experiments, indicating that the models require improvement.
safety_implication: Accurate prediction of flame spread is critical for spacecraft fire growth models and designing effective response strategies; overpredicting or underpredicting spread can compromise crew safety.
evidence: Models predict higher spread rates than observed, so need improvement.
earth_application: Improves combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems on Earth.

finding: BASS-II test data enabled the calculation of combustion completeness, heat release rates, and fuel-to-oxygen global equivalence ratios, as well as supporting theoretical models for quenching boundaries.
safety_implication: Understanding heat release rates and quenching boundaries helps in establishing safe operational envelopes and designing reliable fire suppression systems for spacecraft.
evidence: Data also allowed calculation of combustion completeness, heat release rates, and fuel-to-oxygen global equivalence ratios and supported theoretical models for quenching boundaries.
earth_application: Advances fire detection and suppression on Earth.

finding: Microgravity data allowed scientists to determine thin and thick fuel spread rates and derive a formula for the transition from thin to thick fuels.
safety_implication: Understanding fuel thickness effects on flame spread improves materials flammability screening and helps predict fire growth for different spacecraft components.
evidence: With data from microgravity, scientists determined thin and thick fuel spread rates and a formula for transition from thin to thick fuels.
earth_application: Guides materials flammability screening and understanding of fuel thickness combustion behavior on Earth.

finding: BASS-II aims to improve spacecraft fire safety and material selection by studying combustion in microgravity.
safety_implication: Enables engineers to select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions where a fire can be catastrophic.
evidence: A primary goal of BASS-II is improved spacecraft fire safety, improved understanding of combustion in space and how to avoid it. If you’re on a mission far from Earth, a fire can be catastrophic. BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods on future space missions.
earth_application: Helps researchers evaluate computer models of fuel burning which can be used to study flames on Earth, such as in wildfires, building fires, and energy recapture from waste recycling.

finding: In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as seen on Earth.
safety_implication: Provides a simpler combustion process in microgravity to evaluate computer models of fuel burning.
evidence: In outer space, fuels burn as oval balls rather than with an upward pointed cone flame as they do on Earth. This simpler combustion process enables researchers to evaluate computer models of fuel burning.
earth_application: Enables evaluation of combustion models for terrestrial fires and industrial combustion.

finding: Forty-one test samples are burned across a variety of flow conditions for a total of 89 test points during BASS-II operations.
safety_implication: Extensive testing conditions help characterize material flammability and suppression limits across operating envelopes.
evidence: Forty-one test samples will be burned in a variety of flow conditions for a total of 89 test points.
other_measurements: Test samples: 41; Test points: 89

finding: BASS-II airflow is adjustable from 5 to 50 cm/s, nitrogen vitiation uses station GN2 at a flow rate of up to 500 cc/min, and flames are allowed to burn for about a minute before nitrogen suppressant is applied until extinguishment.
safety_implication: Determines the suppression effectiveness and extinction thresholds of nitrogen on solid fuel flames under controlled microgravity airflows.
evidence: The crewmember adjusts the airflow from 5 to 50 cm/s. Nitrogen vitiation of the working volume is then initiated using station GN2 at a flow rate of up to 500 cc/min for a prescribed time. The flame is ignited and allowed to burn for about a minute. ... adjusts the flow of nitrogen suppressant through the nozzle until the flame goes out.
extinction_threshold: Nitrogen suppressant flow until flame goes out
