other_measurements: Airflow rate: 5 to 50 cm/s; Nitrogen GN2 flow rate: up to 500 cc/min; Burn duration: about a minute
earth_application: Informs suppression system design and agent delivery requirements for enclosed environments.

finding: The BASS-M investigation utilizes modified SPICE hardware in the Microgravity Science Glovebox on the ISS to observe burning solid materials.
safety_implication: Understanding how treated and untreated textiles burn in microgravity helps ensure crew safety and improves fire prevention and material selection on spacecraft.
evidence: The Burning and Suppression of Solids-Milliken (BASS-M) investigation utilizes slightly modified Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) hardware within the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) for observations of burning solid materials on board the International Space Station (ISS).
fuel_material: Textiles (44 samples total across 11 types, including control samples)
fuel_geometry: Textile samples with integrated igniter wires
earth_application: Improves fire safety standards for textiles and clothing used in terrestrial environments.

finding: BASS-M tests 44 textile samples, where a flame from an ignited untreated textile piece impinges on an immediately adjacent treated textile sample.
safety_implication: Evaluates the efficacy of flame-retardant treatments on textiles when exposed to a direct flame impingement in microgravity.
evidence: BASS-M consists of 44 textile samples with integrated igniter wires. There are four samples of each textile type, of which there are eleven. A set of control samples are included which provide untreated textile samples. The other ten sets of textile samples share a similar configuration. Each has a small piece untreated textile which is ignited by an integrated hot wire igniter. The flame from the untreated textile impinges on the treated textile which is immediately adjacent to the untreated sample.
fuel_geometry: Small piece of untreated textile adjacent to a treated textile
earth_application: Helps develop better flame-retardant clothing and interior materials on Earth.

finding: Key experimental observations include flame shape, appearance, spread rate, dynamics, and time to extinction as a function of material and airflow.
safety_implication: Provides critical data for validating combustion and extinction models to predict spacecraft fire behavior accurately.
evidence: The important experimental observations from BASS-M, with respect to the burning process, include flame shape and appearance as a function of flow speed, flame spread rate (how fast the flame develops), and flame dynamics (pulsations, oscillations, etc.). With respect to extinction, the critical observations and data to be collected are the time to extinction as a function of textile material and air flow.
earth_application: Enhances fire dynamics modeling and material flammability testing protocols.

finding: BASS-M tests ten different treated textiles at various air flow rates in microgravity to evaluate their ability to self-extinguish compared to normal terrestrial behavior.
safety_implication: Understanding how microgravity alters self-extinguishing behavior helps validate whether ground-based material screening accurately ensures crew safety in space.
evidence: BASS-M tests ten different treated textiles at various air flow rates found in forced convection in microgravity environments, or in a free fall environment. Each textile’s ability to self-extinguish is evaluated and compared against normal terrestrial behavior.
variables: ten different treated textiles at various air flow rates
earth_application: Benefits materials science research on Earth regarding flame-retardant material behavior.

finding: Forty-four test samples are burned in a variety of flow conditions during BASS-M operations.
safety_implication: Extensive testing across varied flow conditions ensures robust flammability data for spacecraft material selection.
evidence: Forty-four test samples are burned in a variety of flow conditions for a total of 44 test points.

finding: During BASS operations, airflow is adjustable from 5 to 50 cm/s using a fan and measured with an anemometer inside a small flow duct.
safety_implication: Controlling and measuring airflow precisely allows for accurate recreation of forced convection environments found in spacecraft ventilation systems.
evidence: During BASS operations, a fan produces a co-flow of air through the duct. An anemometer is used to measure the actual flow rate. The crew member adjusts the airflow from 5 to 50 cm/s.

finding: Untreated textile is ignited and impinges on the treated textile until both extinguish, taking about a minute.
safety_implication: Measures the time and conditions required for flame propagation to be successfully halted by treated materials in microgravity.
evidence: The untreated textile is ignited and allowed to impinge on the treated textile until both extinguish, which takes about a minute.
other_measurements: time: about a minute

finding: Spherical flames in microgravity with ethylene flowing from a porous sphere into quiescent air exhibit glowing soot trapped within the blue hydrocarbon flame, along with a bright arc of large soot particles in the foreground.
safety_implication: Understanding soot formation and behavior in microgravity is critical for predicting fire hazards, particulate generation, and combustion products in spacecraft environments.
evidence: Spherical flame in microgravity with ethylene flowing from a porous sphere into quiescent air. Glowing soot is trapped within the blue hydrocarbon flame, while a bright arc of large soot particles can be seen in the foreground.
earth_application: Improves industrial burner design and soot emission modeling.

finding: Candle flames exhibit noticeably different shapes and combustion behaviors when burning in Earth gravity compared to 0-g conditions.
safety_implication: Gravity-driven buoyancy strongly alters flame structure, meaning Earth-based flammability tests cannot be directly relied upon for spacecraft fire safety.
evidence: Candle flames: burning in earth gravity (left) in comparison to one burning in 0-g (right).
earth_application: Enhances understanding of buoyant diffusion flames.

finding: A 2-cm diameter acrylic sphere burning in microgravity at 17 percent oxygen and 10 cm/s flow displays occasional yellowish-red streaks caused by vapor bubbles forming in the solid and igniting as they burst through the blue flame.
safety_implication: Boiling and bubble formation inside burning solid polymers in microgravity can cause spurts of burning vapor, creating unexpected flame flickering or accelerated burning hazards in spacecraft.
evidence: A snapshot of 2-cm diameter acrylic sphere burning in microgravity at 17 percent oxygen and 10 cm/s flow from the Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) experiment conducted on the International Space Station. Occasional yellowish-red streaks appear as vapor bubbles formed in the solid are ignited as they burst through the blue flame.
variables: Oxygen concentration at 17 percent, flow velocity at 10 cm/s
earth_application: Improves fire safety standards for plastic materials used in enclosed environments.

finding: The flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity, implying that terrestrial standards for inert gas suppressants in low gravity do not offer the same margin of safety as in normal gravity.
safety_implication: Terrestrial standards for inert gas suppressants do not provide an equivalent margin of safety in low-gravity environments like spacecraft.
evidence: The research to date has shown that the flammability limit is lower in reduced gravity. The implication is that terrestrial standards for inert gas suppressants in low gravity do not offer the same margin of safety as in normal gravity.
earth_application: Physical and chemical kinetic models of heptane and methanol combustion serve as building blocks for models of practical liquid fuels such as diesel and jet fuel.

finding: The smoke-point serves as an effective indicator of a fuel's propensity to emit light and to produce soot, driven by fuel chemistry and flow conditions.
safety_implication: Understanding smoke points helps in predicting soot emissions and mitigating fire hazards and smoke accumulation in spacecraft.
evidence: The smoke-point is a result of the fuel chemistry and flow conditions and is an effective indicator of the propensity of a fuel to emit light and to produce soot
earth_application: Soot control remains a major unsolved problem in combustion and engine development.

finding: The SLICE investigation examines lifting and lifted flames where combustion chemistry and flow conditions cause the flame to detach from the burner and stabilize downstream, with the purpose of increasing fuel efficiency and reducing pollutant emissions.
safety_implication: Advanced combustion modeling allows system designers to improve efficiency and reduce harmful pollutants.
evidence: The SLICE investigates the structure of lifting and lifted flames where flow conditions and the combustion chemistry cause the flame to detach from the burner and stabilize at a downstream position. The twin purposes for the SLICE research are increased fuel efficiency and reduced pollutant emission in practical combustion devices.
earth_application: Improves fuel efficiency and reduces harmful pollutants in terrestrial practical combustion devices.

finding: The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels using a flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel to improve fundamental understanding of materials flammability, ignition, and extinction behavior in low- and partial-gravity environments.
safety_implication: Assessing existing flammability test methods ensures reliable spacecraft fire prevention and materials selection for Moon and Mars missions.
evidence: Specifically, BRE’s objective is to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as ignition and extinction behavior, and assess the relevance of existing flammability test methods for low- and partial-gravity environments.
fuel_geometry: flat porous burner simulating solid and liquid fuels
partial_g_applicability: Assesses the relevance of existing flammability test methods for partial-gravity environments like Moon and Mars.
earth_application: Efficiently measures burning rate over a wide range of fuel properties, helping ascertain flammability test validity.

finding: The CLD Flame experiment aims to develop and experimentally verify chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels by examining normal coflow flames of diluted methane and ethylene in an air coflow under varying injection velocity and fuel dilution.
safety_implication: Improving predictive capabilities for sooty and dilute flames helps prevent unpredicted fire hazards in spacecraft combustion environments.
evidence: The general goal of the CLD Flame experiment is to extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels.
earth_application: Applicable to practical combustion issues such as turbulent combustion, ignition, and flame stability.

finding: E-FIELD Flames investigate how high-voltage electric fields (up to 10 kV) can influence combustion ions to modify flame shape, alter soot or flammability limits, direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutant emission.
safety_implication: Electric fields could potentially be used as active controls or suppression mechanisms for non-premixed flames in space.
evidence: An electric field will be generated by creating a high-voltage (up to 10 kV) differential between the burner and a flat, circular mesh suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.
fuel_geometry: normal coflow flame or simple gas-jet flame
earth_application: Reduces pollutant emissions and controls non-premixed flames.

finding: In the 2.2-second Drop Tower, a spherical diffusion flame test was conducted with 1.51 mg/s of 100 percent ethylene issuing from a porous burner into air at atmospheric pressure.
safety_implication: Understanding soot inception limits aids in designing soot-free combustion systems for spacecraft.
evidence: The gas from the burner was 1.51 mg/s of 100 percent ethylene issuing into air at atmospheric pressure.
fuel_geometry: spherical diffusion flame on a porous burner
other_measurements: gas flow rate: 1.51 mg/s
earth_application: Enables optimization of oxygen-enriched combustion and design of efficient, low-polluting burners.

finding: A partially premixed spherical flame test in the 2.2-second Drop Tower used a gas mixture issuing from a porous burner consisting of 25 percent propane, 2 percent oxygen, 49 percent argon, and 24 percent nitrogen.
safety_implication: Provides fundamental insight into spherical flame extinction limits and dynamics under microgravity.
evidence: The gas issuing from the burner was 25 percent propane, 2 percent oxygen, 49 percent argon, and 24 percent nitrogen.
fuel_geometry: spherical flame on a porous burner
variables: various inert diluents in fuel and chamber atmosphere
earth_application: Advances predictive capabilities for structure and dynamics of both soot-free and sooty flames.

finding: In low-flow microgravity or partial gravity conditions, some solid materials are flammable at lower oxygen concentrations than in normal gravity due to reduced natural convective cooling.
safety_implication: Spacecraft materials may pose higher fire risks than indicated by standard 1-g quiescent tests because ventilation flows and low-flow environments enhance flammability.
evidence: In the low-flow conditions of microgravity or partial gravity, some materials are flammable at lower oxygen concentrations than in normal gravity (Figure 8).
variables: ambient oxygen concentration and forced/buoyant flow velocity
partial_g_applicability: Applies to partial gravity environments such as the Moon or Mars where convective cooling is altered.
earth_application: Informs flammability testing standards and fire safety limits in closed-environment or low-flow terrestrial settings.

finding: Under slow convective flow in microgravity, flames over solid fuels can preferentially spread upstream into the oncoming airflow, which is opposite to normal gravity behavior.
safety_implication: Flame spread direction changes in microgravity mean crew response strategies must account for upstream propagation against ventilation flow.
evidence: Once established, flames in low-speed airflows may preferentially spread into the oncoming airflow (Figure 9) depending on the flow speed. This is opposite to the effect that occurs in normal gravity.
earth_application: Improves fire propagation modeling in confined spaces or forced ventilation environments on Earth.

finding: BASS experiments conducted using the SPICE flow duct in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox burned flat samples, PMMA spheres, porous wax slabs, and wax candles at oxygen levels down to 17 percent using nitrogen dilution.
safety_implication: Demonstrates the effectiveness of nitrogen suppression and flow-velocity effects on solid materials in spacecraft environments.
evidence: Several types of solid materials were burned including flat samples, polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) spheres, porous wax slabs and wax candles. ... more recently nitrogen has been used to perform tests as low as 17 percent oxygen.
fuel_geometry: flat samples, spheres, porous slabs, and candles
variables: oxygen concentration adjusted via nitrogen and flow-velocity
earth_application: Aids in developing better material flammability standards and fire suppression protocols.

finding: Burning a 2-cm diameter acrylic sphere at 17 percent oxygen and 12 cm/s flow caused the flame to stay bluer much longer due to delayed soot formation, facilitating model comparisons of flame growth rate, flame-to-fuel distance, and solid regression rate.
safety_implication: Soot delay at reduced oxygen concentrations alters radiative feedback and burning dynamics of plastics in spacecraft fires.
evidence: Flame sequence of a burning 2-cm diameter acrylic sphere at 17 percent oxygen and 12 cm/s flow from the Burning and Suppression of Solids experiment. ... With the reduction in oxygen from 21 percent (air) to 17 percent, the flame stays bluer much longer (soot formation is delayed) facilitating comparison with model.
other_measurements: burn duration: sequence images about 1.5 s apart
variables: oxygen concentration (17% vs 21%) and flow velocity (12 cm/s)
earth_application: Improves combustion modeling for industrial polymer burning and safety standards.

finding: A cotton-fiberglass fabric (2-cm wide) burned in opposed flow while flow was decreased in discrete steps from 10 cm/s down to less than 1 cm/s exhibited very rapid flame responses and dramatic changes in spread rate over a 90-second total burn time.
safety_implication: Highlights extreme sensitivity of fabric flame spread rates to cabin ventilation velocity changes.
evidence: Digital still camera images showing a flame burning a 2-cm wide cotton-fiberglass fabric in opposed flow. Images are taken every 1.25 seconds ... The flow is decreased in discrete steps from 10 cm/s all the way down to less than 1 cm/s. The flame response to flow changes is very rapid, and the flow effects on the flame and its spread rate are dramatic. Total burn time is 90 seconds.
other_measurements: total burn time: 90 s; image interval: 1.25 s
variables: flow velocity stepped from 10 cm/s down to < 1 cm/s
earth_application: Improves fabric fire safety and flammability testing protocols in variable-flow environments.

finding: The BASS investigation examines the burning and extinction characteristics of fuel samples in microgravity within the MSG to improve 1-g fire safety ratings and guide microgravity fire suppression strategies.
safety_implication: Improves spacecraft fire safety and suppression design by filling knowledge gaps on solid combustion in microgravity.
evidence: The BASS investigation is currently being conducted in the MSG to examine the burning and extinction characteristics of a wide variety of fuel samples in microgravity (Figures 11-13).
earth_application: Will guide combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth.

finding: Nitrogen suppressant applied to a microgravity fire can inadvertently strengthen the flame due to oxygen entrainment depending on geometry and extinguisher characteristics.
safety_implication: Highlights that standard 1-g fire suppression tactics can be hazardous in microgravity if they entrain oxygen and strengthen the fire.
evidence: Depending on the geometry of the flame and the characteristics of the extinguisher (distance from flame, dispersion angle), it is possible that the suppressant stream will be ineffective or might actually make the flame worse through the entrainment of oxygen.

finding: Drop-tower results suggest that the current NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 might not be conservative for spacecraft materials flammability limits.
safety_implication: Indicates a potential safety gap in current spacecraft material screening protocols, requiring updated safety margins.
evidence: It will also provide an increased margin of safety for materials flammability based upon a slightly modified NASA Test 1 protocol, since recent drop-tower results suggest that the current Test 1 might not be conservative.
fuel_material: actual engineering materials planned for spacecraft

finding: Under low-flow conditions below buoyancy-induced velocities, ignition times reach values significantly lower than those observed in normal-gravity buoyant flows due to reduced surface heat loss.
safety_implication: Demonstrates that spacecraft atmospheres with low ventilation flows can have critically reduced ignition times and increased flammability hazards.
evidence: At airflow velocities below those induced by buoyancy, ignition times reach values that are significantly lower than those observed in normal-gravity buoyant flows. The reduction of the ignition times indicates that, under these low-flow conditions, the ignition process is affected more by the reduction in surface heat loss than by the corresponding oxygen transport reduction.

finding: The critical heat flux for ignition in microgravity can be as short as half the value measured in normal gravity.
safety_implication: Materials may ignite much more easily under spacecraft reduced-gravity environments than ground-based testing indicates.
evidence: By developing a theoretical model for the ignition time, it was also shown that the critical heat flux for ignition in microgravity can be as short as half the value measured in normal gravity.

finding: The Water Mist Fire Suppression experiment investigated how water droplet diameter and water concentration affect the speed, strength, and shape of flames created in various fuel and oxygen mixtures.
safety_implication: Findings led to the design, testing, fabrication, and certification of non-toxic water-mist portable fire extinguishers for spaceflight to replace CO2 units on the ISS.
evidence: The purpose of the Mist experiment was to study how water droplet diameter and water concentration affect the speed, strength and shape of flames created in various fuel and oxygen mixtures. After years of research, testing, flight experiments, and advocating the benefits of water-mist technology, non-toxic water-mist portable fire extinguishers were designed, tested, fabricated and certified for spaceflight.
variables: water droplet diameter and water concentration
earth_application: Development of more effective mist fire-suppression systems to replace banned Halon systems.

finding: The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) examined the particle-size distribution of the smoke from spacecraft materials to aid spacecraft fire detection design.
safety_implication: Providing useful guidance for the designers of future spacecraft smoke detectors to achieve rapid detection with limited false alarms.
evidence: The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) examined the particle-size distribution of the smoke from spacecraft materials. These instruments can provide useful guidance for the designers of future spacecraft smoke detectors.

finding: Drop tower testing of Super-Critical Water Oxidation (SCWO) using a 500-ml reactor showed that microgravity conditions result in significant thermal stratification with a hot zone established between two cooler regions, indicating poor thermal mixing compared to normal gravity.
safety_implication: Understanding buoyancy effects on SCWO is critical for designing reliable closed-loop life-support systems for waste management and resource reclamation in space missions.
evidence: In normal gravity, temperatures were found to be more uniform in the bulk fluid, which is due to buoyant mixing; whereas, nonuniformities resulting in thermal stratifications (evidenced by a “hot zone” between two cooler regions) were observed under microgravity conditions.
earth_application: Optimization of terrestrial Super-Critical Water Oxidation reactors for waste destruction.

finding: Long-duration microgravity testing aboard the Russian Mir space station demonstrated that candle flames can burn for over 45 minutes before extinguishing from a lack of fuel, burning to a lower ambient oxygen mole fraction than on Earth.
safety_implication: Disproves the assumption that steady diffusion flames cannot exist without buoyancy, highlighting unexpected fire hazards in spacecraft environments.
evidence: The candle flames in Figure 1 show images of a familiar shape seen in normal gravity and a flame during a microgravity test aboard the Russian Mir orbiting station. Contrary to published speculation, the microgravity flame burned in some tests for over 45 minutes before extinguishing from a lack of fuel. Despite having a much lower burning rate... the microgravity flame burned to a lower ambient oxygen mole fraction than the identical candle flame would have on Earth.

finding: The SOFBALL experiment proved that stationary, spherical premixed flames (flame balls) can exist in microgravity, producing extremely weak flames around 1 Watt with some burning for over 40 minutes.
safety_implication: Demonstrates unique low-energy combustion limits that must be accounted for in spacecraft fire safety and flammability limits.
evidence: Their existence, however, was thought to be a strictly mathematical exercise. The SOFBALL studied premixed fuel/oxidizer/diluent mixtures in a large combustion chamber and showed conclusively that the flames could exist (Figure 14), producing the weakest flames ever burned (approximately 1 Watt) and some burning for over 40 minutes before the experiment timed out (e.g. Ronney, et al., 1998).
other_measurements: power: 1 W

finding: At low-characteristic velocities (low-flame stretch), radiative loss begins to dominate, leading to flame extinction at sufficiently low velocities or stretch rates.
safety_implication: Understanding radiative extinction limits helps determine absolute flammability boundaries for spacecraft materials.
evidence: At low-characteristic velocities (low-flame stretch), radiative loss begins to dominate, eventually leading to flame extinction at sufficiently low velocities or stretch rates (e.g., Olson et al., 1988).
variables: gas velocity across the solid surface and ambient oxygen mole fraction
earth_application: Improves modeling of radiative extinction in low-speed terrestrial fires.

finding: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is not conservative, as materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth.
safety_implication: Current material screening protocols may approve flammable materials for spaceflight use.
evidence: Recent results from the BASS experiment currently running on the ISS indicate that NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is not conservative, and materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth.

finding: Local application of suppressant is inadequate for flame extinguishment because the local jet entrains air and sustains the flame even when ambient airflow is turned off.
safety_implication: Standard local suppressant delivery mechanisms may fail to extinguish spacecraft fires due to air entrainment.
evidence: Also, current findings show that local application of suppressant is not adequate for flame extinguishment. The local jet entrains air and sustains the flame even when the ambient airflow is turned off.

finding: After visible hot flame extinction, droplets continue to vaporize and are supported by a lower-temperature cool flame before vaporization suddenly stops at a finite droplet size.
safety_implication: Unrecognized cool flames can continue fuel vaporization and generate unburned fuel vapor clouds in spacecraft.
evidence: Inexplicably after hot flame extinction, however, the droplet continued to vaporize at the same rate for an extended period and then suddenly stopped vaporizing at a finite droplet size. The plateau in vaporization occurred coincident with the formation of a large vapor cloud. This vaporization, we now know, is supported by a lower-temperature cool flame that forms after visible flame extinction.
earth_application: Improves understanding of cool flame chemistry for internal combustion engines.

finding: FLEX and FLEX-2 experiments exploit microgravity to study spherically symmetric combustion of liquid droplets, identifying radiative and diffusive extinction limits for heptane and methanol droplets.
safety_implication: Understanding droplet extinction limits and limiting oxygen indices helps improve spacecraft fire prevention strategies and inert-gas suppressant effectiveness.
evidence: FLEX and the follow-on FLEX–2 experiments are exploiting the microgravity environment to study the spherically symmetric combustion of liquid droplets. FLEX is motivated by the need to better identify and predict limiting oxygen indices (LOIs) and inert-gas suppressant efficacy. To date, these experiments have identified both the radiative and diffusive extinction limits for heptane and methanol droplets
earth_application: Better understand droplet combustion as it applies to fundamental problems of energy conversion and utilization where liquid hydrocarbon fuels are a predominant source of energy.

finding: Experiments identified limiting oxygen indices (LOIs) that are significantly lower than in normal gravity and lower than previously predicted and anticipated.
safety_implication: Lower actual LOIs than anticipated mean materials could burn in more oxygen-diluted environments than previously assumed, posing a hidden fire safety hazard for spacecraft cabin designs.
evidence: identified an LOI that is both significantly lower than in normal gravity and lower than previously predicted and anticipated.
earth_application: Development, refinement, and validation of chemical kinetic models important to terrestrial combustion systems.

finding: Stable, quasi-steady cool flames form after radiative extinction of the visible flame for heptane droplet combustion.
safety_implication: Cool flames burn at low temperatures without visible light, creating a hidden fire and toxic hazard in spacecraft environments that standard optical flame detectors might miss.
evidence: The most significant observation from these experiments, however, is the identification of stable, quasi-steady cool flames that form after radiative extinction of the visible flame for heptane droplet combustion (Nayagam et al., 2012).
earth_application: Low-temperature chemistry is important in automobile engines because it is one of the major phenomena limiting engine efficiency.

finding: ACME hardware accommodates experiments with burner-stabilized, partially premixed flames and gas-jet diffusion flames to develop and validate chemical kinetic models.
safety_implication: Enables better predictive tools for combustion system safety and efficiency in both space exploration vehicles and terrestrial systems.
evidence: The ACME hardware that is now in development will accommodate experiments with burner-stabilized, partially premixed flames. The ACME investigations, planned to follow the FLEX experiments, examine gas-jet diffusion flames.
earth_application: Relevant to nearly all terrestrial combustion systems and modern gas turbine combustion.

finding: Proposed Microgravity Wind Tunnel for the ISS MSG enables testing of large solid fuel samples to study fire growth patterns, material flammability compared to NASA STD-6001 Test 1, fire suppression, and post-fire cleanup.
safety_implication: Improves spacecraft material selection and fire safety verification using realistic sample sizes and flow conditions expected in future spacecraft.
evidence: This facility would enable large samples to be used to study fire growth patterns, materials flammability compared to NASA’s STD-6001 Test 1, fire suppression testing, and post-fire cleanup applied research.
earth_application: Improves material flammability evaluation and fire risk assessment methods.

finding: Reduced-gravity environments are conducive to low-temperature combustion regimes marked by weak, persistent, invisible cool flames that can spontaneously re-ignite long after visible flames are extinguished.
safety_implication: Invisible cool flames present a hidden crew safety hazard on spacecraft as they can spontaneously re-ignite after apparent extinction.
evidence: reduced-gravity environments have been shown to be particularly conducive to a low-temperature combustion regime marked by very weak but persistent flames, invisible to the unaided eye, that will spontaneously re-ignite long after the visible flame has been extinguished.
earth_application: Relevance to next-generation engine designs such as Homogeneous Charged Compression Ignition and Reactivity Controlled Compression Ignition that rely on low-temperature combustion.

finding: Smoke particles that form in microgravity can be larger than those formed on Earth.
safety_implication: Understanding that microgravity smoke particles are larger aids in calibrating smoke detectors to ensure timely and reliable fire detection for crew safety.
evidence: One thing we have learned is that smoke particles that form in microgravity can be larger than those formed on Earth.

finding: DAFT data indicated low levels of particulate in the International Space Station (ISS) relative to Shuttles.
safety_implication: Baseline particulate levels help in establishing thresholds for ambient air quality monitoring and anomaly detection.
evidence: Data indicated low levels of particulate in ISS relative to Shuttles – not surprising given ISS’s smaller crew size and its filtration system.

finding: Results show average particle sizes are larger on orbit than on Earth.
safety_implication: Account for larger particle sizes when designing spacecraft particulate sensors to prevent detection failures during incipient fires.
evidence: Results show average particle sizes are larger on orbit than on Earth, perhaps due to inefficiency of
earth_application: Helps correlate particle coagulation and growth behaviors between terrestrial and space environments.

finding: Sensitivity to the alcohol content of the atmosphere on board the ISS limits usage of the P-Trak to a maximum of three test points per day.
safety_implication: Restricts operational procedures for particulate and smoke detection on the ISS to avoid false readings or instrument saturation.
evidence: Sensitivity to the alcohol content of the atmosphere on board the ISS limits usage of the P-Trak to a maximum of three test points per day.

finding: At high oxygen concentrations, chemical times are small relative to characteristic flow times, causing droplets to burn to completion rather than exhibiting flame extinction.
safety_implication: Understanding that high oxygen environments like EVA pre-breathing spaces lead to complete droplet combustion rather than extinction helps define the high-risk boundaries for spacecraft fire safety.
evidence: At high oxygen concentrations, however, the chemical times are small enough (relative to the characteristic flow times) such that the droplets will burn to completion rather than exhibiting flame extinction.
variables: Oxygen Mole Fraction, Diluent, Suppressant Type
partial_g_applicability: Applicable to reduced gravity environments during space exploration where atmospheric oxygen and pressure conditions vary.
earth_application: Improves large-scale realistic fire simulations and safety model development for terrestrial combustion applications.

finding: Ambient pressure does not significantly influence the droplet burning rate, but it influences chemistry at sufficiently low values.
safety_implication: Understanding pressure effects on droplet burning supports low-pressure spacecraft habitat depressurization strategies for fire extinction.
evidence: Ambient pressure does not significantly influence the droplet burning rate but does influence chemistry at sufficiently low values.
partial_g_applicability: Applies to spacecraft cabin depressurization scenarios in reduced gravity environments.
earth_application: Useful for understanding fire suppression and burning behavior under reduced pressure industrial environments.

finding: Methanol and heptane are selected as hydrocarbon and alcohol fuels to provide a wide range of fire scenarios and radiative characteristics for model verification.
safety_implication: Testing diverse fuels ensures that fire extinction and suppression models are robust across different material behaviors.
evidence: The study will use two typical hydrocarbon fuels, an alcohol, methanol (CH3OH) and an alkane, heptane (C7H16). There is a relatively large experience base with these fuels. Methanol has a fuel-bound oxygen atom and burns with a very dim blue flame (not much soot production) with a small standoff distance, so it has widely different radiative characteristics than heptane.
partial_g_applicability: Applicable to spacecraft fuel combustion hazards.
earth_application: Assists in modeling the combustion and extinguishment of different liquid fuels found in terrestrial industrial applications.

finding: Initial droplet size varies between 2 and 5 mm to determine deviations from quasi-steady behavior during droplet combustion and extinction.
safety_implication: Accounting for initial droplet size variations helps accurately predict extinction limits across different fuel droplet sizes.
evidence: The initial droplet size in the proposed study will vary between 2 and 5 mm.
partial_g_applicability: Relevant to microgravity droplet combustion where initial droplet size affects transient burning phases.
earth_application: Improves drop-size dependent spray combustion and fire extinction models.

finding: In the absence of gravity, small fuel droplets with diameters from 2 mm to 4 mm burn one-dimensionally with a spherical flame resembling a large olive centered around the droplet.
safety_implication: Understanding single droplet combustion in microgravity provides baseline combustion behaviors without the convective distortions of 1-g, aiding spacecraft fire safety design.
evidence: In the absence of gravity, small droplets of fuel (i.e., from 2 mm to 4 mm in diameter) burn “onedimensionally”, which means the flame will be shaped a like ball about the size of a large olive that will be centered around the droplet.
fuel_geometry: Spherical droplet, 2 mm to 4 mm in diameter
earth_application: Improves modeling of spray combustion in transportation and industrial burners.

finding: During FLEX-2 experiments, dispensed and deployed single droplets or droplet pairs are ignited in a known and controlled gaseous environment, where they either burn to completion or extinguish at a finite state.
safety_implication: Extinction and burning behavior data for droplets help establish flammability limits and containment protocols for liquid fuels in spacecraft.
evidence: The Fundamental Studies in Droplet Combustion and Flame Extinguishment in Microgravity – 2 (FLEX-2) experiments involve dispensing, deploying and igniting either a single droplet or a pair of droplets, depending on the experiment configuration, in a known and controlled gaseous environment. The ignited droplets either burn to completion or the flame extinguishes at a finite
fuel_geometry: Single droplet or pair of droplets
variables: Single droplet or a pair of droplets configuration
earth_application: Enhances industrial liquid fuel burner efficiency and fire safety codes.

finding: In binary droplet array experiments, two droplets are placed along a support fiber at known locations, ignited simultaneously, and their subsequent burning is recorded.
safety_implication: Understanding multi-droplet interactions and binary droplet array combustion helps assess fire spread risks involving multiple fuel droplets in spacecraft environments.
evidence: During the experiments involving binary droplet arrays, two droplets are placed along a support fiber at known locations and the droplets are ignited simultaneously and the subsequent burning is recorded.
fuel_geometry: Two droplets placed along a support fiber
partial_g_applicability: Applicable to spacecraft fire safety where liquid fuels may form droplets or arrays.
earth_application: Improves foundational combustion models for spray combustion, industrial fuel systems, and droplet array hazards.

finding: Convective flow tests subject a single tethered droplet to a known and controlled sub-buoyant flow by moving the fiber crosshairs through the quiescent atmosphere.
safety_implication: Evaluating droplet combustion under convective flow informs how ventilation flows in spacecraft cabin air systems affect burning liquid droplets.
evidence: In the convective flow tests, a single droplet is subjected to a known and controlled sub-buoyant flow of the quiescent atmosphere around the droplet. The flow is realized when the droplet is tethered to a substrate. In this tethered mode the droplet is placed at the intersection of two fiber crosshairs. The cross hairs are then moved through the quiescent atmosphere surrounding the droplet.
fuel_geometry: Single tethered droplet at the intersection of two fiber crosshairs
variables: convective flow velocity and ambient atmosphere
partial_g_applicability: Relevant to forced ventilation flows in spacecraft compartments.
earth_application: Enhances understanding of droplet combustion behavior in forced convective environments such as industrial burners and engines.

finding: FLEX-2 experiments are categorized into pure fuel experiments, fuel mixture experiments, convective flow experiments, and binary droplet array experiments, each involving 30 to 60 separate tests.
safety_implication: Comprehensive testing across multiple fuel types and configurations provides robust data for establishing flammability limits and material selection guidelines.
evidence: The experiments in FLEX-2 can easily be categorized into four separate groupings; these being, the pure fuel experiments, the fuel mixture experiments, the convective flow experiments, and the binary droplet array experiments. Each of these groupings are sponsored by one or more investigators comprising the investigation team and entail anywhere from 30 to 60 separate tests using different fuels, different ambient conditions, or different droplet configurations.
fuel_geometry: Pure fuels, fuel mixtures, single droplets, or binary droplet arrays
variables: fuels, ambient conditions, and droplet configurations
partial_g_applicability: Essential for establishing spacecraft fire safety standards across diverse liquid fuel types.
earth_application: Provides baseline data for liquid fuel safety and fire prevention standards.

finding: The FLEX-2J experiment observes and measures fuel droplet motions during flame spreading along a one-dimensional droplet array composed of fixed and movable droplets on a silicon carbide fiber.
safety_implication: Studying flame spread along droplet arrays helps evaluate the risk of fire propagation through dispersed liquid fuel droplets in microgravity vehicles.
evidence: FLEX-2J will observe and measure fuel droplet motions during flame spreading along a one-dimensional droplet array. Three droplets will be deployed to fixed positions upon ceramic beads on a silicon carbide fiber. Then an additional three to ten movable droplets are positioned to the fiber at known locations.
fuel_geometry: One-dimensional array of 3 fixed and 3 to 10 movable droplets on a silicon carbide fiber
partial_g_applicability: Directly addresses microgravity flame spread mechanisms across droplet arrays.
earth_application: Improves fire propagation modeling for industrial spray systems and fuel leaks.

finding: In the FLEX-2J experiment, the first fixed droplet is ignited to propagate the flame down the array while recording the subsequent burning, unpinned droplet motions, velocities, flame leading edge position, flame spread limit span, and group flame growth process.
safety_implication: Detailed tracking of flame spread limits and droplet velocities provides critical metrics for early fire detection and hazard mitigation strategies in spacecraft.
evidence: The first fixed droplet is ignited, and the flame is propagated down the array from droplet to droplet. The subsequent burning and motions of the unpinned droplets are recorded; particularly the velocities of the free droplets before and after flame spread are measured. In addition, the experiment will obtain the history of flame leading edge position, flame spread limit span, and the growth process of the group flame along the fuel droplet array.
variables: droplet spacing and initial ignition point
partial_g_applicability: Provides essential microgravity data on group flame behavior and droplet propulsion mechanisms.
earth_application: Aids in understanding multi-droplet combustion and flame propagation hazards in industrial settings.

finding: The FLEX-ICE-GA experiment will test surrogate biologically derived fuels (biofuels), specifically 50-50 mixtures of n-heptane/ethanol and 50-50 n-hexanol/n-decane, within the CIR in the FLEX-2 configuration.
safety_implication: Evaluating novel green energy fuels and biofuels helps understand their combustion and flammability characteristics for safe transport and utilization in future spacecraft systems.
evidence: The FLEX-Italian Combustion Experiment for Green Air will test surrogate fuels as defined by the Italian Space Agency (ASI) within the CIR in the FLEX-2 configuration.

finding: Hydrocarbon fuels typically produce soot, plastics produce droplets of recondensed polymer fragments, and paper and silicone rubber produce smoke comprised of liquid droplets of recondensed pyrolysis products.
safety_implication: Understanding that different spacecraft materials produce distinct types of smoke particles aids in designing detectors capable of sensing diverse fire signatures.
evidence: For example, hydrocarbon fuels typically produce soot, and plastics produce droplets of recondensed polymer fragments. While paper and silicone rubber produce smoke comprised of liquid droplets of recondensed pyrolysis products.

finding: SAME will assess the size and distribution of smoke particles produced by spacecraft materials such as Teflon, Kapton, cellulose, and silicone rubber.
safety_implication: Characterizing particle size distributions for specific spacecraft materials ensures that current and future smoke detection systems are sensitive to actual on-orbit fire hazards.
evidence: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) will assess the size and distribution of smoke particles produced by different types of material found on spacecraft such as, Teflon, Kapton, cellulose and silicone rubber.

finding: A substantial portion of the aerosol mass from smoke samples is contained in particles that are larger than 1 micron.
safety_implication: Understanding that large particles contribute significantly to aerosol mass impacts how optical and scattering-based smoke detectors are calibrated and designed for spacecraft safety.
evidence: A substantial portion of the aerosol mass is in particles that are larger than 1 micron.
fuel_material: Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cellulose, and dibutyl-phthalate
variables: airflow rates, heating temperatures, and smoke aging durations
partial_g_applicability: Applies to reduced gravity environments like the ISS, Moon, and Mars.
earth_application: Submarines or underwater laboratories

finding: Teflon smoke primarily comprises particles having diameters of less than 1 micrometer.
safety_implication: Material-specific particle size distributions mean that some overheated materials produce finer aerosols requiring specific detector types.
evidence: Teflon smoke comprised primarily of particles having diameters less than 1 um.
partial_g_applicability: Applies to reduced gravity environments.
earth_application: Submarines or underwater laboratories

finding: The effect of aging on smoke is consistent with particle coagulation and limited wall loss, leading to a substantial decrease in the overall number count while mass concentrations remain relatively steady.
safety_implication: Smoke aging over time in a closed spacecraft cabin alters particle characteristics, which affects how long detectors can reliably sense the smoke before properties shift.
evidence: The effect of aging is consistent with particle coagulation with limited wall loss, the overall number count decreases substantially while the mass concentrations remain relatively steady.
partial_g_applicability: Applies to microgravity and reduced gravity environments.
earth_application: Submarines or underwater laboratories

finding: Although arithmetic mean diameters for silicone rubber smoke are in the 227 nm range, almost half of the particle mass is larger than 1000 nm due to a broad size distribution.
safety_implication: Relying solely on arithmetic mean diameter can be misleading for detector design since larger particles disproportionately affect light scattering signals.
evidence: Consequently, although the AMD for silicone rubber is 227 nm, almost half the particle mass is larger than 1000 nm.
other_measurements: arithmetic mean diameter: 227 nm
partial_g_applicability: Applies to microgravity and reduced gravity environments.
earth_application: Submarines or underwater laboratories

finding: All tested samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulates better detected using an ionization smoke detector, though a light scattering detector performs very well for most cases.
safety_implication: Combining ionization and light scattering technologies or using multi-spectrum detectors can enhance early fire detection reliability in spacecraft.
evidence: All samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are better detected using an ionization smoke detector, however a light scattering detector would perform very well for most of the cases.
fuel_material: Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cellulose, and dibutyl-phthalate
sensors: ionization smoke detector, light scattering detector
partial_g_applicability: Applies to microgravity and reduced gravity spaceflight.
earth_application: Submarines or underwater laboratories

finding: The SAME-R flight experiment utilized a thermal precipitator for collecting smoke particles for Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), several aerosol instruments, and a commercial smoke detector to measure moments of the particle size distribution.
safety_implication: Measuring the particle size distribution moments helps evaluate spacecraft smoke detector performance and improve early fire detection capabilities for crew safety.
evidence: Repeatable sample surface temperatures were obtained with SAME engineering hardware and measurements were taken with returned flight diagnostic equipment consisting of a thermal precipitator for collecting smoke particles for Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), several aerosol instruments, and a commercial smoke detector.
fuel_material: Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber, Pyrell
sensors: thermal precipitator, commercial smoke detector, aerosol instruments
variables: Different materials (Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber, and Pyrell) tested in ground and flight.
partial_g_applicability: Applies to microgravity spacecraft fire detection systems.
earth_application: Improves smoke characterization and detector testing for enclosed environments on Earth.

finding: Soot particles dominate established flaming fires, whereas unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer fragments are produced by smoldering and pyrolysis during the early stages of fire growth.
safety_implication: Targeting early-stage pyrolysis products rather than established flaming soot is critical for spacecraft fire detection due to constrained crew quarters and early warning requirements.
evidence: Soot particles dominate the smoke particulate in established flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer fragments are produced by smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fire growth.
partial_g_applicability: Critical for confined spacecraft environments where early detection prevents catastrophic fire growth.
earth_application: Enhances early-stage fire and smoldering detection in residential and industrial buildings on Earth.

finding: Spacecraft fire detection systems target the early phase of fire growth (pyrolysis products) rather than established flaming fires due to constrained spacecraft spaces.
safety_implication: Focusing on early pyrolysis products ensures prompt alarm before fire escalation in crewed spacecraft.
evidence: Given the constrained space on any spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is pyrolysis products rather than soot.
partial_g_applicability: Addresses microgravity spacecraft volume constraints and emergency response times.
earth_application: Relevant to enclosed or isolated environments on Earth such as submarines or aircraft.

finding: Historical spacecraft smoke detection systems faced limitations, including line-of-sight and false alarm issues in Skylab UV-detectors, and particle size filtering in Space Shuttle and International Space Station detectors.
safety_implication: Understanding historical sensor limitations (such as missing particles outside specific size ranges) guides the design of more robust multi-parameter detection systems for future exploration missions.
evidence: The Skylab module, however, included approximately 30 UV-sensing fire detectors. These devices were limited to line-of-sight and were reported to have difficulties with false alarms. The Space Shuttle Detectors were based upon ionization fire detector technology, the most advanced technology available at the time and used an inertial separator designed to eliminate particles larger than 1-2 µm. The International Space Station (ISS) smoke detectors use near-IR forward scattering, rendering them most sensitive to particles larger than 1 µm

finding: Six component failures by overheating or other causes occurred in the NASA Orbiter fleet, along with several similar incidents on the ISS.
safety_implication: As mission durations increase, the likelihood of spacecraft component failures increases, underscoring the critical need for improved fire detection.
evidence: As described by Friedman, there have been six component failures by overheating or other causes in the NASA Orbiter fleet in addition to several similar incidents that have occurred on the ISS.

finding: The 1997 fire incident on Mir demonstrated that failures of oxygen generation systems can have significant consequences.
safety_implication: Oxygen generation system failures pose severe hazards in spacecraft environments, driving the need for enhanced fire detection systems.
evidence: The experience on Mir in 1997 has shown that failure of oxygen generation systems can have significant consequences.

finding: Microgravity combustion experiments show that fire can behave very differently in space compared to Earth, requiring different fire prevention, detection, and suppression methods.
safety_implication: Spacecraft fire safety systems cannot rely solely on Earth-derived methods and must account for altered microgravity fire behavior.
evidence: However, microgravity combustion experiments have shown that fire can behave very differently in space and the best methods to prevent, detect, and extinguish fires on a spacecraft may be very different than those used on Earth.
earth_application: Understanding microgravity combustion helps improve combustion theory and fire safety generally.

finding: Different fuels produce distinct smoke types in spacecraft: hydrocarbon fuels produce soot, overheated plastics produce recondensed polymer fragment droplets, and paper and silicone rubber produce liquid droplets of recondensed pyrolysis products.
safety_implication: Spacecraft smoke detectors must be capable of detecting diverse particulate types resulting from different potential spacecraft materials.
evidence: Hydrocarbon fuels typically produce soot, while overheated plastics produce droplets of recondensed polymer fragments. Paper and silicone rubber produce a smoke that is composed of liquid droplets of recondensed pyrolysis products.
fuel_material: hydrocarbon fuels, plastics, paper, silicone rubber
earth_application: Improves smoke detection algorithms for various building and industrial materials on Earth.

finding: The Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment demonstrated that solid particulate smokes created in microgravity formed longer chains and aggregated into larger particles than those created in normal Earth gravity.
safety_implication: Microgravity soot aggregation alters particle size distribution, directly affecting the response and reliability of spacecraft smoke detectors.
evidence: The Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment that flew in the Glovebox on STS-75 demonstrated that the smokes with solid particulates created in microgravity formed longer chains, and aggregated into larger particles than those created in normal Earth gravity.
sensors: ISS smoke detector, STS smoke detector
earth_application: Enhances understanding of soot agglomeration dynamics in flames.

finding: Increased residence time in high-concentration smoke regions in microgravity caused solid particulates to form longer chains and larger particles.
safety_implication: Altered particle sizing impacts the detection thresholds and performance of existing spacecraft fire detection hardware.
evidence: This is surmised to have occurred because of the increased residence time in the high concentration smoke regions and to have affected the responses of the two spacecraft smoke detectors (ISS and STS) utilized in that experiment.
sensors: ISS smoke detector, STS smoke detector
earth_application: Aids in modeling particulate transport and smoke aging in confined spaces.

finding: The SAME experiment aims to quantify sizes of liquid smoke particulates in microgravity and relate droplet size and distribution to smoke generation and transport conditions.
safety_implication: Provides critical data for designing advanced smoke detectors capable of distinguishing between dust and smoke in spacecraft.
evidence: The major goal of this experiment is to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulates achieve in microgravity and to relate the droplet size and distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment.
earth_application: Improves particulate matter sensing technology for commercial and industrial applications.

finding: Measurements will be made of three moments of particle size distribution for microgravity smoke from several spacecraft materials considering sample temperature, air flow, smoke residence time, and smoke aging.

finding: In microgravity, condensed alcohol droplets inside the P-Trak may form a film that bridges and blocks the nozzle or gets trapped in an optics chamber, causing sensor failure or false high counts.

evidence: In microgravity, the distinct possibility exists that these droplets will form a film that will bridge and block the nozzle, effectively plugging the flow of droplets and preventing the device from functioning, or obscuring the optics. Furthermore, there is some concern that the droplets inside the optics chamber may get trapped in an internal circular motion and be counted more than once, producing an erroneously high count.

finding: Machining 60 0.006-inch grooves down the length of the inside of the condenser was implemented to allow fluid to wick back to the reservoir via capillary action, replacing gravity-driven drainage.
safety_implication: Provides a passive engineering control for liquid management in particle counters operating in weightlessness.
evidence: The modification that was implemented in order to counteract these potential problems was: 60. 0.006” grooves were machined down the length of the inside of the condenser. These grooves were designed to provide a mechanism in which the smoke particle/ alcohol mixture can wick its way back to reservoir end to simulate the effects of gravity, hence, inhibiting the possibility of the fluid to inhibit the functioning of the unit.

finding: The Dynamic Diluter uses a laminar flow element and differential pressure transducer to control and dilute aerosol samples, reaching the desired dilution setpoint in approximately 5 seconds.

evidence: In the event of loss of power all solenoids will close including the mass flow controllers, therefore the system will not over pressurize.

evidence: The pyrolysis products of Teflon currently have a JSC Tox level 3 for 5 minutes after creation. After this point the particles coalesce and drop to tox level 0.
other_measurements: JSC Tox level: 3 for 5 minutes then drops to 0

finding: Smoke is contained within the smoke tube and aging chamber for 5 minutes and expelled through HEPA filters into the ISS vent or MSG, with MSG operating under negative pressure.
safety_implication: Multi-barrier containment and HEPA filtration prevent toxic smoke and pyrolysis products from contaminating the spacecraft cabin atmosphere.
evidence: The smoke is contained in the smoke tube and aging chamber for 5 minutes. All the smoke is expelled through HEPA filters, some of which dumps into the ISS vent the rest of it into the MSG. The MSG is the second containment of the smoke if the aging chamber where to leak. Finally the MSG is under a negative pressure which would prevent the smoke from leaking in the event of an MSG leak.

finding: The ISS Smoke Detector, P-Trak, and DustTrak utilize fully contained Class 1 lasers meeting ANSI Z136.1-2000 standards with no crew access at any time.

evidence: The ISS Smoke Detector, the P-Trak and the DustTrak contain lasers as a part of their diagnostics systems. These lasers are of Class 1 lasers, and the laser beams are fully contained. evidence: This investigation completed 250 combustion tests with various fuel mixtures, including propylene, propane, and ethylene, in microgravity. Researchers identified more than 70 smoke points, which yielded estimates of soot-forming conditions and flame dimensions.
