finding: During Saffire-IV, researchers burned SIBAL cloth (75% cotton and 25% fiberglass), observing bright speckles of glowing char behind the spreading flame.
safety_implication: Observing char behavior and flame spread characteristics on cotton-fiberglass composites aids in material screening for Moon and Mars spacecraft.
evidence: During the Saffire IV experiment, researchers burned a sample of SIBAL cloth, a composite of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass. As the flame spreads shortly after ignition, you can see bright speckles behind, which are glowing char on the cloth.

finding: Saffire-V examines fire growth in the range of pressures and oxygen concentrations expected in future exploration spacecraft.
safety_implication: Testing fire growth under realistic exploration atmospheric conditions ensures future spacecraft fire safety measures are reliable.
evidence: Saffire-V examines fire growth in the range of pressures and oxygen concentrations expected in future exploration spacecraft.
partial_g_applicability: Applies to future exploration spacecraft atmospheres

finding: Saffire-VI tests flammability at different oxygen levels and demonstrates fire detection, combustion product monitoring, and post-fire cleanup capabilities.
safety_implication: Demonstrating detection, monitoring, and cleanup capabilities in microgravity directly enhances crew safety and environmental control system design for deep-space missions.
evidence: Saffire-VI, the last of the series, builds on previous results from Saffire-I through V to test flammability at different oxygen levels and to demonstrate fire detection, combustion product monitoring, and post-fire cleanup capabilities.

finding: Laminar diffusion flames detach and lift above (move downstream of) the nozzle under specific flow conditions, which enables excellent agreement with accurate numerical modeling.
safety_implication: Understanding flame detachment and stabilization helps improve combustion modeling, which reduces design time and cost for practical spacecraft combustion devices and fire safety systems.
evidence: In particular, excellent agreement can be achieved when the flow conditions are such that the flame detaches and lifts above (i.e., moves downstream of) the nozzle. A coupled experimental and numerical investigation can enable validation and improvements to combustion modeling.
partial_g_applicability: Microgravity testing allows for greater temporal and spatial scales and a broader range of flame characteristics compared to normal gravity.
earth_application: Improves combustion modeling for terrestrial combustion devices and fire safety systems.

finding: Flame attachment point controls the stability of the entire trailing diffusion flame, making attachment or detachment of essential importance in fire safety.
safety_implication: Controlling or predicting flame attachment is critical for managing flame stability and preventing unintended fire propagation in spacecraft environments.
evidence: Furthermore, flame attachment to (or detachment from) a burner or condensed-fuel surface is of essential importance in both combustion systems and fire safety. The flame attachment point controls the stability of the entire trailing diffusion flame.
earth_application: Applicable to flame stability control in terrestrial burners and industrial fires.

finding: Microgravity testing allows for greater temporal and spatial scales and a broader range of flame characteristics than can be achieved in normal gravity.
safety_implication: Microgravity enables more detailed observation of combustion dynamics that might be compressed or obscured under terrestrial gravity conditions.
evidence: Microgravity testing allows for greater temporal and spatial scales and a broader range of flame characteristics than can be achieved in normal gravity.
partial_g_applicability: Provides expanded temporal and spatial scales for flame analysis under microgravity.
earth_application: Fundamental insights apply to microgravity drop-tower or space station research benefiting Earth combustion understanding.

finding: The SLICE study targets diffusion flames of methane, ethylene, and selected nitrogen dilutions burning in a coflow of air to characterize structure from attached through lifted conditions and to identify liftoff velocity limits.
safety_implication: Characterizing flame structure and liftoff limits as a function of fuel, burner diameter, and flow conditions improves quantitative fire risk assessment for spacecraft.
evidence: For diffusion flames of methane, ethylene, and selected nitrogen dilutions of each fuel burning in a coflow of air: (1) Characterize the structure of the flame, especially its base (i.e., stabilizing region), from attached through lifted conditions as a function of the fuel, burner diameter, and flow conditions. (2) Identify the liftoff velocity limits as a function of the fuel and burner diameter.
fuel_material: methane, ethylene, nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene
variables: fuel type, nitrogen dilution, burner diameter, flow conditions
partial_g_applicability: Conducted in microgravity to evaluate flame liftoff velocity limits and structure.
earth_application: Aids in understanding fundamental combustion limits and flame stabilization in terrestrial burners.

finding: SLICE operating procedures involve fixing the fuel flow and incrementally increasing the air velocity until the diffusion flame detaches and lifts off from the nozzle.
safety_implication: Understanding flame liftoff and detachment behavior in microgravity improves fundamental combustion safety models and hazard predictions for spacecraft fire scenarios.
evidence: In contrast, SLICE will include testing where the fuel flow is fixed, and the air velocity is incrementally increased until the diffusion flame detaches and lifts off from the nozzle.
fuel_geometry: coflow laminar diffusion flame from nozzle
earth_application: Provides insight into burner safety, flame stabilization, and blow-off limits for industrial combustion systems.

finding: Capturing flame lifting processes in normal gravity is extremely difficult, making microgravity SLICE photographic observations valuable for studying transient flame behavior.
safety_implication: Microgravity testing isolates buoyancy effects, providing cleaner data for validating numerical combustion models used to predict spacecraft fire behavior.
evidence: Given that the capture of the lifting processes in normal gravity is extremely difficult, SLICE will provide valuable photographic observations on the transient flame behavior.
fuel_geometry: coflow laminar diffusion flame from nozzle
earth_application: Improves fundamental scientific understanding of transient combustion phenomena unmasked by buoyancy on Earth.

finding: If the heater offset correction returns a value greater than 50uV, the test must be aborted and restarted.
safety_implication: Ensures that heater offsets are within safe operational limits prior to continuation of thermal tests, preventing uncontrolled thermal excursions or equipment damage.
evidence: If the offset correction returned a value greater than 50uV, abort the test and restart.
partial_g_applicability: Applies to microgravity combustion testing rigs inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG).
earth_application: Reliability and safety protocols for automated resistance-heated combustion and material tests.

finding: The software or operator will abort heating if the sample resistance or temperature exceeds the maximum limits.
safety_implication: Protects against runaway heating, material degradation, and potential fire hazards within the closed MSG environment.
evidence: The software will too, and will abort heating if the resistance/temperature gets too high. But watch anyway and send the Abort command in the highly unlikely event of too high resistance/temperature.
partial_g_applicability: Applies to closed-environment spacecraft combustion experiments.
earth_application: Over-temperature protection mechanisms in automated laboratory furnaces and testing chambers.

finding: The nominal heater control setpoint multiplier Rt/R0 for Kapton sample type is 1.380.
safety_implication: Proper temperature setpoints prevent runaway thermal degradation or incomplete aging during spacecraft materials testing.
evidence: Kapton | 1.380
partial_g_applicability: Applies to thermal degradation and smoke generation testing hardware operated in microgravity on ISS.
earth_application: Material flammability and thermal stress testing procedures.

finding: The nominal heater control setpoint multiplier Rt/R0 for Lampwick sample type is 1.245.
safety_implication: Ensures controlled thermal aging without causing unexpected violent combustion.
evidence: Lampwick | 1.245
partial_g_applicability: Applies to spacecraft materials testing.
earth_application: Material flammability and thermal stress testing procedures.

finding: The nominal heater control setpoint multiplier Rt/R0 for Silicone sample type is 1.327.
safety_implication: Ensures controlled thermal aging without causing unexpected thermal degradation.
evidence: Silicone | 1.327
partial_g_applicability: Applies to spacecraft materials testing.
earth_application: Material flammability and thermal stress testing procedures.

finding: The nominal heater control setpoint multiplier Rt/R0 for Teflon sample type is 1.440.
safety_implication: Ensures controlled thermal aging without causing unexpected thermal degradation.
evidence: Teflon | 1.440
partial_g_applicability: Applies to spacecraft materials testing.
earth_application: Material flammability and thermal stress testing procedures.

finding: Actual inlet velocity must match the desired inlet velocity to within plus or minus 0.5 cm/sec.
safety_implication: Ensures precise control over fluid delivery and aerosol generation rates during experiments.
evidence: Actual inlet velocity is required to match desired inlet velocity to within +/- 0.5 cm/sec.

finding: Piston chamber fill movement begins by evacuating the drive side of the piston at a rate of 3.0 LPM until the drive side pressure reaches 13.2 psia.
safety_implication: Proper pressurization and chamber fill parameters maintain consistent experimental conditions.
evidence: Piston chamber fill movement begins by evacuating the the drive side of the piston at a rate of 3.0 LPM until the drive side pressure reaches 13.2 psia.

finding: The system exhausts at a rate sufficient to achieve overpressure of the diagnostic duct for all combinations of diagnostic use except when using the STS detector with both DustTraks.
safety_implication: Ensures that the diagnostic duct remains properly overpressurized during standard testing configurations, avoiding potential containment or pressure failures during crew operations.
evidence: It was verified that the system exhausts at a rate sufficient to achieve overpressure of the diagnostic duct for all combinations of diagnostic use except when using the STS detector with both DustTraks.

finding: Using ground support equipment, fluid flow during chamber exhaust was insufficient to maintain overpressure of the diagnostic duct when the STS detector and both DustTraks are in use simultaneously.
safety_implication: Inadequate diagnostic duct overpressure during chamber exhaust can compromise smoke and aerosol containment or detection accuracy, presenting a potential monitoring hazard during crew safety evaluations.
evidence: Using ground support equipment there was insufficient fluid flow during chamber exhaust to maintain overpressure of the diagnostic duct, as required, when the STS detector and both DustTraks are in use.

finding: The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project consists of five independent experiments focused on advancing combustion technology through fundamental research.
safety_implication: Enhances fundamental understanding of materials flammability and combustion behavior to improve spacecraft fire prevention and combustion safety.
evidence: The Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project is now under development with a set of five independent experiments which are each focused on advancing combustion technology through fundamental research.
fuel_geometry: one or two dimensional laminar, non-premixed (diffusion) flames using gaseous fuels
sensors: temperature sensors, flame radiation and chemiluminescence sensors, ion current and electric potential sensors
earth_application: Improve efficiency and reduce emissions in practical combustion processes on Earth through better computational models.

finding: Unlike the other current ACME experiments, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is focused on fire prevention, especially in spacecraft.
safety_implication: Improves our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, extinction behavior, and sustained combustion conditions for spacecraft fire safety.
evidence: Unlike the other current ACME experiments, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is focused on fire prevention, especially in spacecraft.
fuel_material: gaseous fuels including mixtures with inert gases to simulate paper, plastic, and alcohol
fuel_geometry: flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel
other_measurements: heats of combustion and gasification, surface temperature, smoke point
earth_application: Assessing relevance of existing flammability test methods.

finding: The Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment extends the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels.
safety_implication: Aids in predicting flame behavior under extreme fuel dilution and sooty pure-fuel conditions, directly applicable to turbulent combustion, ignition, and flame stability.
evidence: The general goal of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is to extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels.
fuel_material: diluted methane and ethylene in an air coflow

finding: Electric fields can strongly influence flames by affecting ions, modifying flame shape, altering soot or flammability limits, directing heat transfer, and reducing pollutant emissions.
safety_implication: Provides a mechanism to control non-premixed flames and manage combustion hazards or pollutant formation using electric fields.
evidence: An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions present as a result of the combustion reactions. The direct ion transport and the induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot or flammability limits, direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutant emission.
other_measurements: ion current: up to 10 kV differential; field strength and fuel dilution
sensors: ion current and electric potential sensors

finding: Flame Design investigates soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames to optimize oxygen-enriched combustion and design robust, soot-free non-premixed flames.
safety_implication: Leads to improved burner designs that are efficient and less polluting by understanding the role of flame structure on soot inception.
evidence: Flame Design will investigate the soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames, created in the same manner as for the s-Flame experiment.

finding: The s-Flame experiment advances the ability to predict the structure, dynamics, and extinction of both soot-free and sooty spherical flames in microgravity.
safety_implication: Identifies extinction limits for radiative and convective extinction and determines pulsating instabilities relevant to combustion safety.
evidence: The purpose of the Structure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame) experiment is to advance our ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction, of both soot-free and sooty flames.

finding: Spherical burners used in Flame Design and s-Flame must have specified fixed outer diameters of 6.4 mm, 9.5 mm, and 12.7 mm within a tolerance of ±0.3 mm.
safety_implication: Standardizing burner geometry ensures reproducible flame behavior and thermal boundary conditions across spaceflight combustion experiments.
evidence: Each spherical burner shall include a porous sphere with a fixed outer diameter. The burner tip diameters shall be 6.4 mm (¼ inch), 9.5 mm (3/8 inch), and 12.7 mm (½ inch) where each is within ±0.3 mm and is measured and known within ±0.1 mm.
fuel_geometry: Porous sphere with outer diameters of 6.4 mm, 9.5 mm, or 12.7 mm
variables: Burner tip diameter (6.4 mm, 9.5 mm, 12.7 mm)
earth_application: Improves reproducibility of burner-stabilized combustion experiments in ground laboratories.

finding: Spherical burners must be capable of withstanding temperatures from 0 to 450 C within 75 mm of their center.
safety_implication: Thermal endurance prevents hardware degradation and structural failure under high-temperature combustion environments.
evidence: Within 75 mm of its center, the burner - including the supply tube - shall be capable of withstanding temperatures of at least 0 to 450 ºC.
earth_application: Applies to high-temperature burner testing safety on Earth.

finding: Gas-jet burner tubes must have a length at least 40 times greater than their inner diameter to establish a parabolic velocity profile at the nozzle tip.
safety_implication: Ensuring well-defined velocity profiles prevents flow instabilities that could compromise combustion diagnostic accuracy.
evidence: The straight tube of constant internal cross-section in a gas-jet burner shall be at least 40 times greater in length than the inner diameter (or width)
earth_application: Applicable to burner nozzle design in industrial combustion research.

finding: Gas-jet burner nozzles must be internally and externally smooth with an average roughness under 100 um, and tips smoothed under 20 um roughness to prevent turbulence and corona discharges.
safety_implication: Minimizing surface roughness prevents unintended electrical arcing and flow turbulence during high-voltage electric field operations.
evidence: Each nozzle shall be internally and externally smooth with an average roughness of no more than 100 μm. The tip shall be free of burs and sharp edges and smoothed to an average roughness of no more than 20 μm
earth_application: Reduces electrical breakdown and arcing risks in high-voltage electrostatic apparatus.

finding: Gas-jet burners must withstand temperatures of at least 0 to 1000 C within 50 mm of their tips.
safety_implication: Prevents thermal failure of burner tips exposed to intense flame zones.
evidence: Within 50 mm of its tip, each gas-jet burner shall be capable of withstanding temperatures of at least 0 to 1000 ºC.
earth_application: Relevant to high-temperature burner durability in industrial settings.

finding: The coflow burner inner tube must maintain a constant 2.1 mm inner diameter for a length of at least 40 times its inner diameter to create a parabolic velocity profile.
safety_implication: Maintains predictable flow characteristics essential for stable coflow flame experiments.
evidence: The inner tube’s inner diameter shall be constant for a length of at least 40 times the inner diameter
earth_application: Improves flow control stability in laboratory coflow burners.

finding: The variation in axial velocity with angular position for the coflow burner must be less than 10% of the mean velocity across all radial positions from 0 to 10 mm.
safety_implication: Ensures axisymmetric flow conditions, preventing asymmetric flame distortions that could invalidate scientific data or cause unexpected thermal loads.
evidence: the variation in axial velocity with angular position shall be less than 10% of the (mean) velocity, where this shall hold for all radial positions from 0 to 10 mm.
earth_application: Guarantees flow quality in standard coflow combustion test rigs.

finding: Gas-jet and coflow burners used as electrodes must have a resistance of less than 1 Ohm along their length and across their outlet surfaces to ensure uniform potential and act as an ion current pathway.
safety_implication: Low electrical resistance ensures that the burner acts as a proper conductive pathway rather than an obstruction for ion currents during electric field experiments.
evidence: Each gas-jet and coflow burner shall have a resistance of less than 1 Ohm along its length and each coflow burner shall have a resistance of less than 1 Ohm across its entire outlet surface, such that each of these burners is electrically conductive and at a nearly uniform potential.
earth_application: Applies to electrostatic combustion control systems and safety grounding.

finding: With an electric field of -10 kV and +10 kV combined with an axial distance of 35 mm between the electrode mesh and burner, the current leakage measured in air at 1 bar must be less than 100 nanoamps.
safety_implication: Limits leakage currents to prevent electrical faults, short circuits, or unintended energy dissipation inside the combustion chamber.
evidence: With an electric field of both -10±0.1 kV and +10±0.1 kV combined with an axial distance of 35±2 mm between the electrode mesh and the burner, the current leakage measured in air (at 1 bar absolute) shall be <100 nanoamps and as small as possible.
fuel_material: Copper mesh and stainless steel burner
other_measurements: current leakage: <100 nA
earth_application: Ensures electrical insulation integrity in high-voltage laboratory setups.

finding: The gas delivery system must control gas mixture compositions to within plus or minus 0.01 mole fraction.
safety_implication: Precise mixture control prevents off-nominal reactant concentrations that could lead to flashback, unexpected flammability limits breaches, or unstable combustion.
evidence: The composition of any mixture shall be controlled to within  0.01 mole fraction and as accurately as possible.
earth_application: Critical for precise gas-blending safety in industrial combustion testing facilities.

finding: Elevated oxygen testing for Flame Design leads to higher flame temperatures which can significantly shorten hot-wire igniter life, suggesting Hot Surface Ignition (HSI) may be preferable.
safety_implication: Selecting appropriate ignition hardware prevents premature igniter failure under high-oxygen combustion test conditions.
evidence: While hot-wire igniters have been effectively used in many combustion experiments, special care is required for ACME because of the testing with elevated oxygen (for the Flame Design experiment) which leads to higher flame temperatures which in turn could significantly shorten igniter life. Hot Surface Ignition (HSI), which is often used in furnaces, may be better for ACME than hot-wire ignition.
earth_application: Ignition reliability in high-oxygen industrial or laboratory environments.

finding: Microgravity flames can be highly dependent on small changes of 0.01 mole fraction in oxygen concentration near soot, stability, or extinction limits.
safety_implication: Precise control of ambient gas composition is critical to prevent unintended flame extinction or instability in spacecraft fire research.
evidence: microgravity flames can be highly dependent on small changes (e.g., of 0.01 mole fraction) in the oxygen concentration, especially near soot, stability, or extinction limits
extinction_threshold: oxygen concentration changes of 0.01 mole fraction
earth_application: Precision gas mixture control in closed-environment combustion systems.

finding: Testing shall not be conducted during thruster firings or spacecraft dockings/undockings based on SPICE results, while normal ISS operations provide adequate acceleration environments with PaRIS isolation.
safety_implication: Isolating combustion experiments from spacecraft impulsive maneuvers ensures consistent gravity-jitter free data collection.
evidence: Testing shall not be conducted when thruster fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS. Based on SPICE results, the normal ISS operations should otherwise provide an adequate acceleration environment, especially given that the CIR is equipped with a Passive Rack Isolation System (PaRIS).
earth_application: Minimization of vibrational and acceleration disturbances in sensitive laboratory combustion rigs.

finding: BRE burners require a circular gas-permeable outlet plate 5.3±0.1 mm thick acting as a thermally-thin calorimeter with at least 60 holes in a uniform circular arrangement.
safety_implication: Standardized burner head design ensures consistent heat flux measurements and repeatable boundary conditions for spacecraft flame spread and burning rate emulation.
evidence: Each BRE burner’s outlet plate shall be 5.3±0.1 mm thick (and as such it will act as a thermally-thin calorimeter) and it shall have at least 60 holes across the entire outlet surface, with uniform diameters of no more than 1/15th of the burner diameter
fuel_geometry: circular gas-permeable plate 25 and 50 mm in diameter, 5.3 mm thick
earth_application: Standardized burner design for laboratory material flammability and heat release rate testing.

finding: The BRE burner top plate must have an emissivity of at least 0.85 for 0.6-15 um to minimize the burner heating transient from flame heat and reduce variations from soot deposition.
safety_implication: High emissivity prevents cumulative thermal drift and soot absorption artifacts during long-duration spacecraft combustion runs.
evidence: On its outlet surface (i.e., face), each BRE burner’s top plate shall have an emissivity of at least 0.85 and as high as possible for 0.6-15 µm. The two purposes for the high emissivity are (1) to minimize the burner heating transient (i.e., from the heat of the flame) and (2) to minimize changes in the burner properties over time by reducing the dependence of the thermal absorption on soot deposition.
earth_application: Design of durable, soot-resistant burner faces for industrial combustion monitoring.

finding: Having two camera views allows confirmation that flames are axisymmetric and permits different optical setups for imaging dim blue chemiluminescence versus hot soot regions without saturation.
safety_implication: Enables accurate monitoring of flame shape and high-temperature regions, ensuring early detection of anomalies during spacecraft combustion experiments.
evidence: Having two views would allow for confirmation that flames are axisymmetric. Two views could be set differently, where one camera could image the dim blue of the flame (while saturating in the hot soot region), where the second camera could be set to image the hot soot region without saturation, making it useful for soot pyrometry.
variables: Camera view settings and optical filtering
partial_g_applicability: Applies to microgravity spaceflight combustion studies where buoyancy-free flame behavior must be characterized.
earth_application: Improves optical diagnostic techniques for industrial combustion monitoring and fire safety research.

finding: An optical filter configuration utilizing a BG7 Schott glass filter reduces blackbody soot emission relative to chemiluminescent blue emission to prevent camera saturation.
safety_implication: Prevents detector blinding during high-soot combustion tests, ensuring reliable optical observation of flame structure.
evidence: to reduce the blackbody soot emission (e.g., red) relative to the chemiluminescent emission (e.g., blue) to avoid saturation while maintaining sensitivity to the much dimmer chemiluminescent emission
earth_application: Enhances flame visualization systems in high-soot industrial furnaces.

finding: Temperature measurements on the spherical burner surface must be between 20 and 90 degrees of the burner tube, verified via drop tower testing to ensure probes do not disturb flame symmetry.
safety_implication: Validates that physical sensors do not artificially alter microgravity flame behavior, ensuring accurate hazard assessment.
evidence: The spherical burner surface temperature shall be measured at a location between 20 and 90 of the burner tube. If the measurement is made with a probe, then the probe shall not be visible during testing in at least one view of the color imaging for data analysis. If a probe is used, then 2.2 Second Drop Tower testing shall be conducted with conditions approved by the Project Scientist to verify that the probe doesn’t affect the visible symmetry of the flame
partial_g_applicability: Tested via drop tower to simulate microgravity effects on probe flow interaction.
earth_application: Ensures non-intrusive sensor placement in delicate combustion test rigs.

finding: Probes for gas-jet and spherical burners must be smaller than 250 microns to minimize flow and flame disturbance.
safety_implication: Minimizes aerodynamic and thermal perturbation of microgravity flames by diagnostic hardware.
evidence: If the measurement involves a probe, the probes for the gas-jet and spherical burners shall each be smaller than 250 microns and as small as possible.
earth_application: Improves micro-sensor design for minimal flow disruption in laboratory burners.

finding: Flame extinction is automatically detected using a combination of photomultiplier tube measurements and color imaging to trigger operational sequences.
safety_implication: Provides automated control triggers for extinguishing or altering tests when flames fail or reach extinction limits.
evidence: Flame extinction will be determined by a combination of two diagnostics: photomultiplier tube measurements and color imaging. Flame extinction shall be automatically detected and will typically trigger a step in the operational sequence.
partial_g_applicability: Applicable to spacecraft automated fire response systems.
earth_application: Improves automated fire detection and suppression trigger systems.

finding: The Hamamatsu H5784-06 was demonstrated in 1g testing to be approximately one to two orders of magnitude more sensitive than the human eye when viewing blue and yellow ethylene Santoro burner flames at 120 mm.
safety_implication: Ensures optical diagnostic equipment selected for spacecraft fire detection exceeds human visual response baselines.
evidence: In 1g testing at NASA Glenn (conducted by Amy Mielke in 2001), the Hamamatsu H5784-06 was shown to be approximately one to two orders of magnitude more sensitive than the human eye where blue and yellow ethylene Santoro burner flames were viewed at a distance of about 120 mm.
earth_application: Improves flame sensor design and sensitivity specifications for terrestrial combustion monitoring systems.

finding: The ion current amplitude measurement range must be at least 0 to 25 microamps.
safety_implication: Defines sensor operating limits for monitoring electrical characteristics and soot production in spacecraft diffusion flames.
evidence: The amplitude of the ion current measurement shall be over a range of at least 0 to 25 microamps.
earth_application: Standardizes electrical diagnostic ranges for terrestrial combustion research burners.

finding: The maximum acceptable sensor body temperature for Space Shuttle Flight Qualified heat flux units is 600 degrees F (316 degrees C).
safety_implication: Establishes thermal structural limits for heat flux instrumentation hardware to prevent sensor failure during flight operations.
evidence: It is important to note that the maximum acceptable sensor (body) temperature is 600  F (316  C) for the Space Shuttle Flight Qualified units.
earth_application: Provides temperature ceiling guidelines for heat flux transducers used in high-temperature industrial environments.

finding: Schmidt-Boelter thermopile type heat flux transducers shall be used because they exhibit small temperature variations compared to Gardon type sensors.
safety_implication: Ensures accurate heat transfer analysis by minimizing sensor surface temperature variation effects.
evidence: The heat flux onto the outlet surface of each BRE burner shall be measured with the Schmidt-Boelter thermopile type of heat flux transducer because this type has a small temperature variation whereas the alternate Gardon type has a large temperature difference across the surface which adversely affects the heat transfer and analysis of results.
earth_application: Improves heat flux measurement accuracy in terrestrial fire testing apparatuses.

finding: The measurement range for the heat flux sensors shall be 0 to 50 kW/m2.
safety_implication: Defines the required operational envelope for quantifying thermal radiation and convection loads in spacecraft burner tests.
evidence: The measurement range shall be 0-50 kW/m2 .
earth_application: Establishes calibration ranges for heat flux sensors in industrial fire safety testing.

finding: For Open Loop Sensing and Control tests, ion current and luminosity fluctuations along with flame images are collected across voltage steps and ramps.
safety_implication: Understanding electric field effects on combustion allows better control strategies for spacecraft fire safety and suppression system design.
evidence: Ion current and luminosity (broadband and CH*) fluctuations will be collected as well as flame images.
sensors: PMT, video cameras, ion current sensors
partial_g_applicability: Microgravity research supporting spacecraft safety.
earth_application: Optimizing combustion efficiency and controlling pollutant formation in industrial burners.

finding: Spherical Flame Design tests evaluate the soot-inception limit while continuously recording temperature distributions.
safety_implication: Characterizing soot limits helps prevent unexpected smoke and soot hazards during spacecraft fires.
evidence: Allow the flame to pass its soot-inception limit. Continuously record temperature distributions.
variables: fluent gas composition and flow rate
partial_g_applicability: Applicable to partial-g and microgravity fire prevention.
earth_application: Improving soot prediction models in terrestrial combustion systems.

finding: Spherical Flame Design radiative extinction tests utilize a PMT or near real-time video to detect extinction, followed by a flow reduction to confirm.
safety_implication: Establishing extinction boundaries aids in understanding fire suppression limits in spacecraft environments.
evidence: Detect radiative extinction with a PMT or with near real-time video. Continuously record temperature distributions.
partial_g_applicability: Applicable to spacecraft fire safety design.
earth_application: Enhancing fire extinction protocols and suppression agent design.

finding: BRE operational tests halt fluent flow if heat flux sensors exceed a critical temperature of 300C or if the flame extinguishes.
safety_implication: Critical temperature limits protect hardware and prevent uncontrolled thermal runaway or secondary fires in spacecraft.
evidence: Anytime during this step, if the flame extinguishes, or either heat flux sensor exceeds a critical temperature of 300oC, then proceed immediately to step 7 (e.g., halting the flow).
other_measurements: sensor temperature: 300 oC; burner surface temperature: 250 oC
partial_g_applicability: Applicable to spacecraft combustion experiments.
earth_application: Thermal protection systems and automated shutoff controls for industrial burners.

finding: For methane and nonsooting ethylene flames, lift-off heights decrease by about a factor of two due to the higher laminar flame speed of ethylene, but this does not cause burner heating.
safety_implication: Understanding burner heating risks during high-speed laminar flame experiments prevents equipment damage on spacecraft.
evidence: The laminar flame speed of ethylene is higher than that of methane, causing lift-off heights to decrease by approximately a factor of two. For nonsooting flames, this decrease in lift-off height does not create any burner heating.
other_measurements: lift-off height decrease: factor of two
variables: fuel type (methane vs ethylene) and dilution
earth_application: Optimizing burner thermal management in ground-based combustion studies.

finding: Heavily sooting ethylene flames cause moderate heat transfer to the burner surface due to soot propensity, especially under microgravity.
safety_implication: Microgravity conditions increase soot propensity and decrease lift-off heights, elevating the risk of hardware thermal damage.
evidence: However, the more heavily sooting cases have been observed to cause moderate heat transfer to the burner, which becomes a problem in the ethylene flames since they have a higher propensity to soot, particularly at microgravity.
variables: gravity level and fuel sooting propensity
partial_g_applicability: Microgravity enhances soot propensity and reduces lift-off height, exacerbating burner heating risks.
earth_application: Managing radiative and conductive thermal loads on burners in industrial sooting flames.

finding: A 50% C2H4 / 50% N2 dilution level ensures a room temperature boundary condition at the burner surface for computations.
safety_implication: Establishing proper mixture dilution prevents excessive thermal feedback to the burner assembly during spaceflight experiments.
evidence: The 50% C2H4 / 50% N2 flame has been observed to be the lowest level of dilution that ensures the room temperature boundary condition at the burner surface to be a good assumption for the computations.
earth_application: Validating boundary conditions in computational fluid dynamics models for combustion.

finding: The maximum duration of any test in the s-Flame experiment matrix is 25 seconds.
safety_implication: Defines operational test constraints for spaceflight combustion testing in microgravity.
evidence: The maximum duration of any test is 25 s.

finding: Sintered porous metal works best for s-Flame spherical burners compared to porous ceramic or hollow spheres with holes created by EDM.
safety_implication: Using robust spherical burner materials ensures structural integrity and reliable flame production for spacecraft combustion experiments.
evidence: Sintered porous metal apparently works best, rather than porous ceramic or hollow spheres with holes created by EDM.
partial_g_applicability: Applies to microgravity combustion experiments on spacecraft.
earth_application: Design of porous burners for industrial combustion research.

finding: For s-Flame commercial spheres, approximately 30% are acceptable and sometimes only 1 in 10 work out.
safety_implication: Rigorous quality control and screening are necessary to select burners that produce concentric and spherical flames for spacecraft safety experiments.
evidence: For the commercial spheres, perhaps 30% are acceptable. Sometimes, only 1 in 10 work out.
partial_g_applicability: Applies to hardware development for space flight missions.
earth_application: Manufacturing quality control for precision combustion research hardware.

finding: Flame Design spherical burners utilize 10 micron sintered stainless steel with a 6.35 mm outside diameter and 1.59 mm hole diameter.
safety_implication: Standardized burner dimensions ensure consistent flame behavior and repeatability during spacecraft combustion testing.
evidence: Sphere and tube material: stainless steel, Sphere pore size: 10 micron, sintered, Sphere outside diameter: 6.35 mm (0.25 inch), Sphere hole diameter (to center): 1.59 mm (1/16 inch)
partial_g_applicability: Applies to hardware specifications for space exploration missions.
earth_application: Precision burner fabrication for combustion laboratories.

finding: Normal-gravity flames produced by the CLD baseline coflow burner are typically less than 2.5 cm tall with a maximum 1g diameter of about 0.6 cm.
safety_implication: Understanding normal-gravity baseline flame dimensions helps calibrate and scale expectations for microgravity spacecraft fire safety tests.
evidence: The normal-gravity flames produced by this burner are typically less than 2.5 cm tall, with a maximum 1g diameter of about 0.6 cm.
other_measurements: flame height: 2.5 cm; maximum diameter: 0.6 cm
partial_g_applicability: Provides a baseline comparison against microgravity conditions.
earth_application: Ground-based diffusion flame testing and burner benchmarking.

finding: An effective resistance of 200 giga-ohms is recommended for the insulation between the mesh electrode and the chamber to limit leaking current to 0.05 mA at 10 kV.
safety_implication: Proper electrical insulation prevents excessive leakage currents, reducing electrical hazards and measurement errors during high-voltage electric field flame suppression tests in spacecraft.
evidence: An effective resistance of 200 giga-ohms is recommended for the insulation between the mesh electrode and the chamber. With that resistance, leaking current at 10 kV would be 0.05 mA, which is sufficiently small in comparison with estimated flame current of ~ 1 mA.
other_measurements: resistance: 200 giga-ohms; leaking current: 0.05 mA; voltage: 10 kV
partial_g_applicability: Applicable to electric field combustion hardware flown in spacecraft.
earth_application: High-voltage electrical safety design for laboratory combustion chambers.

finding: Recent drop tests indicate an initial heat flux of about 50 kW/m^2 at ignition, which generally drops to about 5 kW/m^2 during tests.
safety_implication: Understanding expected heat flux transients during ignition and steady burn helps protect spacecraft hardware and design adequate thermal protection systems.
evidence: Recent drop tests indicate an initial heat flux of about 50 kW/m^2 at ignition and then generally dropping to values of about 5 kW/m^2.
other_measurements: initial heat flux: 50 kW/m^2; subsequent heat flux: 5 kW/m^2
partial_g_applicability: Applies to microgravity drop tower tests representing spaceflight conditions.
earth_application: Applicable to standard fire development and heat transfer characterization in industrial burners.

finding: Medtherm heat flux sensors can easily over range by 150% within their linear calibration, and their maximum body temperature must not exceed 600 degrees F.
safety_implication: Ensures accurate sensor selection and placement so instrumentation does not fail during high-intensity transient combustion events.
evidence: As the Medtherm sensors can easily over range by 150%, within their linear calibration, the 10 mV limit can be exceeded. The sensor thermocouple specification is sufficient for operation without water, provided the sensor does not exceed 600 ºF (316 ºC), which is the maximum (body) temperature for the Space Shuttle Flight Qualified sensors.
sensors: Medtherm Schmidt-Boelter heat flux transducer, Thermocouple
partial_g_applicability: Directly applies to spaceflight combustion rigs.
earth_application: Applies to rigorous industrial and aerospace instrumentation safety limits.

finding: The Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment uses gas-fueled laminar diffusion flames to extend the range of accurately predictable flame conditions by developing and experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels.
safety_implication: Improving fundamental combustion models helps optimize combustion processes and reduce emissions, contributing to overall design safety and efficiency.
evidence: The general goal of the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment is to extend the range of flame conditions that can be accurately predicted by developing and experimentally verifying chemical kinetic and soot formation submodels.

finding: The Flame Design experiment will investigate soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames using ethylene or methane with various concentrations of fuel and oxygen.
safety_implication: Understanding soot inception and limits in microgravity enables better suppression and hazard prevention for spacecraft fire safety.
evidence: Flame Design will investigate the soot inception and extinction limits of spherical microgravity flames, created in the same manner as for the s-Flame experiment. Tests will be conducted with various concentrations of both the fuel (i.e., ethylene or methane) and oxygen in order to determine the role of the flame structure on the soot inception.
earth_application: Improves burner designs to be efficient and less polluting.

finding: The s-Flame experiment creates spherical flames using a porous spherical burner to identify extinction limits for radiative and convective extinction.
safety_implication: Identifying extinction limits aids in predicting fire growth and ensuring reliable fire suppression systems.
evidence: One experiment objective is to identify the extinction limits for both radiative and convective extinction (i.e., at high and low system Damkohler numbers, respectively).
variables: inert diluents in fuel and chamber atmosphere
earth_application: Enhances prediction of flame structure and dynamics in industrial combustion systems.

finding: An electric field generated by high voltage up to 10 kV between a burner and a mesh can modify flame shape, alter soot limits, direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutants.
safety_implication: Electric fields offer a potential active mechanism to control non-premixed flames and suppress unwanted combustion.
evidence: An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions present as a result of the combustion reactions. The direct ion transport and the induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot or flammability limits, direct heat transfer, and reduce pollutant emission.
earth_application: Pollutant emission reduction and active combustion control in terrestrial burners.

finding: ACME must be capable of carrying out operational functions while simultaneously acquiring imaging and non-imaging data, flowing gas, illuminating the chamber, projecting light, energizing the electric field, and sensing for flame extinction in a time-constant manner.
safety_implication: Ensures simultaneous monitoring and safety controls like automated shutdown remain fully operational during complex combustion tests.
evidence: Unless otherwise specified, ACME shall be capable of carrying out operational functions while simultaneously doing any specified subset or all of the following in a time-constant manner: (1) acquiring imaging and non-imaging data, (2) flowing gas, (3) illuminating the chamber, (4) projecting light from the CIR illumination package, (5) energizing the electric field, and (6) sensing for flame extinction.
sensors: flame extinction sensor, pressure sensor, temperature sensor
partial_g_applicability: Applies to microgravity spaceflight combustion facilities requiring automated safety trips.
earth_application: Reliable integrated control systems for industrial combustion research and safety test chambers.

finding: ACME shall provide a detailed time log of commands issued for each test conducted to assist in determining whether a flame naturally extinguished or was terminated by commanded flow.
safety_implication: Accurate reconstruction of test termination prevents misinterpretation of fire suppression or extinction limits in spacecraft safety analysis.
evidence: ACME shall provide a detailed time log of commands issued (i.e., functions enacted) for each test conducted.
partial_g_applicability: Crucial for analyzing low-gravity combustion behavior where natural extinction limits are narrow.
earth_application: Standard diagnostic logging for combustion test facilities.

finding: ACME shall be capable of cleaning soot off gas-jet burners if unacceptably high leak currents are measured during tests utilizing an electric field.
safety_implication: Prevents electrical short circuits and equipment damage from soot accumulation during high-voltage electric field combustion tests.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of cleaning the soot off of gas-jet burners where this could be necessary if an unacceptably high leak current is measured for the tests with an electric field.
partial_g_applicability: Soot mitigation in closed-loop spacecraft systems where deposits pose hazards.
earth_application: Maintenance of high-voltage electrostatic burners in industrial settings.

finding: ACME shall be capable of venting the CIR chamber atmosphere to a specified pressure within a range of 0.01 to 3 bar.
safety_implication: Enables precise pressure control and emergency depressurization or containment capability in spacecraft combustion hardware.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of venting the CIR chamber atmosphere to a specified pressure within a range of at least 0.01 to 3 bar, with an uncertainty of no more than the greater of 0.01 bar or 1% of the specified pressure
partial_g_applicability: Essential for managing gas mixtures in sealed spaceflight pressure vessels.
earth_application: Pressure vessel management and controlled venting systems.

finding: ACME shall be capable of verifying that the CIR chamber is sealed and gas-tight following any operation where the chamber is opened.
safety_implication: Guarantees cabin containment integrity and prevents hazardous gas leaks into the spacecraft environment after hardware maintenance.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of verifying that the CIR chamber is sealed, i.e., gas tight. This is important for safety following any operation in which the chamber is opened.
partial_g_applicability: Vital for maintaining spacecraft cabin atmospheric safety and pressure containment.
earth_application: Leak testing for hazardous or enclosed industrial test chambers.

finding: All electrically powered CIR and ACME components must be powered up in advance of operation by at least their recommended manufacturer warm-up durations to ensure accurate measurements and proper functioning.
safety_implication: Ensures sensors, controllers (such as Mass Flow Controllers), and safety trips are fully warmed up and responsive before ignition.
evidence: All such devices shall be powered up in advance of operation, including data acquisition, by at least the minimum warm-up durations recommended by their manufacturers so that they function properly and provide accurate measurements, if any.
partial_g_applicability: Ensures critical autonomous safety measurements operate accurately in spaceflight experiments.
earth_application: Proper instrumentation operation protocols in experimental laboratories.

finding: ACME shall be capable of energizing the igniter at a specified voltage within a range of at least 50% to 100% of maximum power for a specified duration and de-energizing it.
safety_implication: Precise control over igniter energy delivery ensures reliable ignition sequences without unexpected thermal excursions during spaceflight combustion experiments.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of energizing the igniter at a specified voltage (with a precision of 2% or less, where a precision smaller than 0.2% is probably more than adequate, and within a range of at least 50% to 100% of the maximum power), for a specified duration... and de-energizing the igniter.

finding: ACME shall be capable of zeroing all ACME mass flow controllers (MFCs) or any specified subset to improve flow control and measurement accuracy.
safety_implication: Zeroing mass flow controllers prevents calibration drift and guarantees precise reactant delivery for combustion safety limits.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of zeroing all ACME MFCs or any specified subset thereof to improve the accuracy of the flow control and measurement .

finding: ACME shall be capable of venting and purging all gas delivery lines or any specified subset thereof.
safety_implication: Venting and purging lines removes hazardous or residual unburnt gases from combustion chambers, preventing accidental backfires or toxic leaks.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of venting all gas delivery lines or any specified subset thereof.

finding: ACME shall be capable of setting all ACME MFCs to specified steady flow rates within a range of 0 to 100% and a precision of 0.1% or less.
safety_implication: High precision steady flow rates are necessary to maintain stable, well-characterized flames and prevent blow-off or flash-back hazards.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of setting all ACME MFCs or any specified subset thereof for specified steady flow rate(s) (within a range of 0 to 100% and a precision of 0.1% or less

finding: ACME shall be capable of stepping flows upward and/or downward with defined step values, wait durations, and cycle counts.
safety_implication: Stepped flow capability allows dynamic testing of flame extinction limits and transient behaviors crucial for spacecraft fire safety boundaries.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of setting all ACME flows or any specified subset thereof to step upward and/or downward by specified value(s)... and pausing to hold all flows steady for a specified wait duration

finding: ACME shall be capable of linearly ramping flows upward and/or downward with specified ramp durations and wait durations for defined cycles.
safety_implication: Linear flow ramping permits smooth transitions across flammability limits without triggering unstable combustion spikes.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of setting all ACME flows or any specified subset thereof to linearly ramp upward and/or downward by specified value(s)... for a specified ramp duration

finding: ACME shall be capable of opening and closing all CIR and ACME solenoid valves or any specified subset thereof.
safety_implication: Solenoid valve control provides immediate isolation of fuel and oxidizer supply lines in the event of an emergency or unexpected fire event.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of opening and closing all ACME solenoid valves or any specified subset thereof.

finding: ACME shall be capable of translating the TFP fiber array at a specified rate up to 100 mm/s to positions within its operational range without touching the burner.
safety_implication: Controlled automated positioning of diagnostics prevents physical damage to experiment hardware or the burner assembly during operations.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of translating the TFP fiber array at a specified rate (as high as at least 100 mm/s with an uncertainty of no more than 0.1 mm/s)... to a position within its operational range which shall extend from at least the center of the CIR chamber window axes (except that it shall not touch the burner)

finding: ACME must be capable of activating the electric field at a specified polarity and voltage ranging from -10 kV to +10 kV with an accuracy of plus or minus 0.1% of the set point.
safety_implication: Enables precise control of electric fields for combustion research and flame modification in spacecraft fire safety experiments.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of activating the electric field at the specified polarity (positive or negative) and voltage with a precision and range at least meeting ISRD 1.7.1. Per the baselined ACME requirements, the electric field shall have a range of (at least) -10 kV to +10 kV with an accuracy of ± 0.1% of the set point.

finding: ACME shall be capable of resetting the electric field potential by a step change without deactivating and reactivating it, maintaining a range of -10 kV to +10 kV.
safety_implication: Maintains system stability and continuous electric field application during rapid experiment adjustments.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of resetting the electric field potential, by a step change, adjusting the polarity (positive or negative) and/or voltage of the electric field (with a precision and range at least meeting ISRD 1.7.1), while the electric field is activated, i.e., without deactivating and reactivating it.

finding: ACME shall be capable of deactivating the electric field safely without requiring parameters.
safety_implication: Provides a direct operational shutdown mode for electric field experiments to ensure crew and hardware safety.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of deactivating the electric field. No parameters are required for this function.

finding: ACME must operate with the electric field polarity alternating at frequencies of up to 100 Hz during stepping functions.
safety_implication: Ensures the capability to study high-frequency alternating electric field effects on combustion dynamics.
evidence: Per the baselined ACME requirements, ACME shall be capable of operating with the polarity alternating at frequencies of up to 100 Hz.

finding: ACME shall be capable of detecting flame extinction after ignition by monitoring non-imaging instruments such as optical sensors, chemiluminescent emission, thermal radiation, or thermopile detectors.
safety_implication: Reliable and rapid extinction detection ensures timely automated response and prevents uncontained combustion anomalies in microgravity.
evidence: ACME shall be capable of detecting flame extinction after ignition, by monitoring one or more specified non-imaging instruments and verifying that time-filtered (e.g., averaged) measurement(s) over a specified duration are beyond specified value(s), and responding to that event.

finding: In response to extinction detection, ACME shall be capable of setting all gas flows to zero after a specified duration.
safety_implication: Provides an immediate automatic mitigation response to extinguish any residual combustion or prevent fuel accumulation.
evidence: In response to extinction detection, ACME shall be capable of setting all gas flows to zero after a specified duration (with a precision of 0.1 s or less, where a precision smaller than 0.01 s is probably more than adequate, and within a range of at least 0.0 to 99.99 s) following extinction detection

finding: In response to extinction detection, ACME must be capable of setting any flows by specified values within a range of 0 to 100% and holding flows at their new values.
safety_implication: Ensures precise automated system responses to flame extinction events during microgravity combustion operations.
evidence: In response to extinction detection, ACME shall be capable of setting any flows by specified value(s) (within a range of 0 to 100% and a precision of 0.1% or less) for a specified ramp duration... and holding the flows at their new values.
earth_application: Automated response and flow control systems for combustion safety tests.

finding: During the Extinction Limit Test procedure, fuel and inert flows are started at uplinked ignition conditions such as a 40% CH4 flame or a 20% C2H4 flame at 0 seconds.
safety_implication: Establishes standard operational parameters for determining extinction limits of methane and ethylene flames under microgravity conditions.
evidence: Start coflow and fuel/inert flow at uplinked ignition condition (e.g., a 40% CH4 flame or a 20% C2H4 flame)
earth_application: Understanding flammability limits and extinction behaviors of hydrocarbon gases.

finding: In the Extinction Limit Test, the test stops when extinction is detected by PMT or when a velocity of 50 cm/s is reached.
safety_implication: Provides explicit stop criteria for preventing uncontrolled combustion or verifying flame blow-off thresholds.
evidence: Stop test when extinction is detected by PMT or 50 cm/s is reached
earth_application: burner safety limits and blow-off detection.

finding: During E-FIELD flame testing, if blowout occurs at any time during voltage sweeping, the voltage must be zeroed and the procedure must proceed to shut off gas flows.
safety_implication: Ensures controlled handling of unexpected flame extinction during high-voltage operations in spacecraft combustion experiments.
evidence: Measure (if blowout occurs anytime; zero voltage and proceed to Step D)
earth_application: Standard laboratory safety protocols for high-voltage combustion burners.

finding: Leakage current is measured by repeating the voltage sweep procedure without a flame present after shutting off gas flows.
safety_implication: Verifies electrical isolation and system integrity to prevent electrical hazards in microgravity hardware.
evidence: Repeat Step C beginning from 0V without flame to measure leakage current. Stop testing and report if leakage is at unacceptable level.
earth_application: Electrical leakage detection in high voltage experimental chambers.

finding: During electric field flame operations, the coflow velocity is increased in progressive steps from 1 cm/s to 25 cm/s with data collected over 3-second intervals.
safety_implication: Understanding flame behavior and soot response under varying flow and electric field conditions helps refine spacecraft fire safety models and detection systems.
evidence: Increase coflow velocity to 1cm/s; collect over 3 sec.
earth_application: Improves fundamental combustion control and understanding of soot dynamics in electric fields for industrial burner safety.

finding: For spherical flame tests in Flame Design, chamber contents require a hold time of 5 minutes to reach quiescent, isothermal, and well-mixed conditions.
safety_implication: Ensures repeatable baseline initial conditions for standardized flammability and extinction testing in spacecraft fire safety verification.
evidence: A hold time of 5 minutes is required for quiescent, isothermal, and well-mixed conditions.
variables: Chamber species compositions and pressure set points
earth_application: Standardizing laboratory combustion and extinction limits testing.

finding: Radiative extinction in Flame Design spherical flame tests is confirmed by reducing the flow rate by an estimated 50% for 5 seconds after initial extinction detection.
safety_implication: Provides a robust operational protocol to verify true radiative extinction versus transient fluctuation in microgravity combustion tests.
evidence: At uplinkable time (estimated 3 s) after extinction, reduce flow rate by uplinkable amount (estimated 50%) for uplinkable time (estimated 5 s) to confirm extinction.
variables: Flow rate reduction duration and magnitude
earth_application: Improving extinction verification methods in fundamental flame research.

finding: Kinetic extinction is evaluated in Flame Design by linearly decreasing the fluent flow rate to zero over a 20 second window following ignition.
safety_implication: Establishes precise operational criteria for determining kinetic extinction limits of gaseous diffusion flames in microgravity.
evidence: After an uplinkable time (estimated 10 s), decrease fluent flow rate linearly in time such that flow rate becomes zero at uplinkable time (estimated 30 s) after ignition.
earth_application: Study of kinetic extinction limits in low-stretch flames.

finding: For s-Flame tests, the spherical diffusion flame is maintained for a duration of 25 seconds or until extinction occurs.
safety_implication: Defines standard test durations for assessing spherical diffusion flame stability and extinction characteristics in microgravity.
evidence: Maintain flow rate with same initial mixture for duration of test (25 s) or until extinction.
other_measurements: duration: 25 s
variables: Constant flow versus single step decrease in flow rate
earth_application: Evaluation of porous burner diffusion flames and soot formation under controlled flows.

finding: Flames have been produced by varying the stoichiometric mixture fraction Zst at constant adiabatic flame temperature that are soot-free at any strain rate (permanently blue) and have extinction scalar dissipation rates up to 40 times those of standard fuel-air counterparts.
safety_implication: Understanding how to produce soot-free, highly extinction-resistant flames can inform the design of safer and more efficient combustion systems in spacecraft.
evidence: By varying Zst at constant Tad, flames have been produced that are soot-free at any strain rate (permanently blue) and have extinction scalar dissipation rates up to 40 times those of their fuel-air counterparts.
extinction_threshold: scalar dissipation rates up to 40 times those of their fuel-air counterparts

finding: Microgravity experiments allow the effects of convection direction and flame structure to be independently varied by ejecting fuel into oxidizer or oxidizer into fuel in buoyancy-free systems.
safety_implication: Separating buoyancy effects from fundamental combustion chemistry provides uncorrupted data to evaluate fire risks and behaviors in microgravity exploration environments.
evidence: This issue can be addressed by performing microgravity experiments because the unique character of nonbuoyant microgravity flames allows the effects of convection direction and flame structure to be independently varied. By ejecting fuel into an oxidizer in a buoyancy free system, the convective flow across the flame is unambiguously from fuel to oxidizer. Alternatively, by ejecting oxidizer into fuel, the flow is from oxidizer to fuel.
variables: convection direction (fuel into oxidizer vs oxidizer into fuel)

finding: Studies indicate there is a unique Zst where the flame is most resistant to extinction, suggesting peak temperature can be shifted to coincide with radical production and allow burning at much lower temperatures.
safety_implication: Identifying extinction limits and low-temperature burning characteristics aids in establishing robust flammability boundaries and fire prevention strategies for spacecraft design.
evidence: Studies of the effect of Zst on scalar dissipation rate at extinction have indicated that there is a unique Zst where the flame is most resistant to extinction. These findings also suggest that by employing inert exchange to vary Zst, the peak temperature can be shifted to coincide with the location of radical production, thus allowing the flame to burn at much lower temperatures.

finding: Microgravity experiments will involve gaseous hydrocarbon diffusion flames supported on porous spherical burners and coflow burners to study soot inception and flame extinction limits.
safety_implication: Provides fundamental data on soot formation and extinction mechanisms without gravity-induced buoyancy interference, improving material selection and fire safety standards.
evidence: Microgravity experiments will involve gaseous hydrocarbon diffusion flames supported on porous spherical burners and coflow burners. Soot inception limits and flame extinction limits will be obtained as functions of Zst, amount of inert, flow direction, and pressure.
variables: Zst, amount of inert, flow direction, pressure

finding: Experimental and numerical studies demonstrated that the stoichiometric mixture fraction Zst has a profound effect on soot inception in diffusion flames.
safety_implication: Manipulating the stoichiometric mixture fraction can control soot and particulate formation, reducing combustion hazards in spacecraft systems.
evidence: Du and Axelbaum (1995) showed experimentally and numerically that Zst can have a profound effect on soot inception.
earth_application: Control of particulate emissions and soot in industrial combustion systems.

finding: Flames remain permanently blue at high Zst even when strain rates or coflow flame heights approach limiting conditions, indicating suppressed soot inception.
safety_implication: Permanently blue flames indicate cleaner combustion with reduced soot production, minimizing smoke and particulate hazards in enclosed spaces.
evidence: Significantly, at high Zst the flames remain blue even when strain rates are small in counterflow flames or as heights approach infinity in coflow flames. G.M. Faeth coined the name permanently-blue to describe such flames (Lin and Faeth, 1996).
earth_application: Designing soot-free burners and industrial furnaces.

finding: In an ethylene/air diffusion flame with Zst = 0.064, mean ethylene concentrations are large in the high temperature region, creating conditions favorable for soot inception.
safety_implication: Standard air-fueled combustion creates favorable conditions for soot and smoke formation, requiring active particulate monitoring and protection.
evidence: Fig. 1.1 indicates that in the ethylene/air flame the mean ethylene concentration is large in the high temperature region, i.e., conditions are favorable for soot inception.
earth_application: Understanding soot formation in standard air-combustion engines.

finding: In a diluted-ethylene/oxygen flame with Zst = 0.78, the mean fuel concentration in the high temperature region is low, inhibiting fuel-pyrolysis chemistry.
safety_implication: Oxygen-enriched or inert-exchanged combustion can prevent fuel pyrolysis and reduce soot hazards.
evidence: However, in the diluted-ethylene/oxygen flame, the mean concentration of fuel in the high temperature region is low. Thus, fuel-pyrolysis chemistry is inhibited at high Zst.
earth_application: Design of advanced clean burners utilizing oxygen enrichment.

finding: Soot-free conditions may be obtainable for many fuels if flame structure is adjusted so significant oxidizer exists on the fuel side at low temperatures.
safety_implication: Understanding soot inception limits particulate production hazards in spacecraft fire environments.
evidence: Du and Axelbaum (1995) suggested it may be possible to obtain soot-free conditions for many fuels if the structure of the flame can be adjusted to the extent that significant oxidizer exists on the fuel side of the flame at a low enough temperature.
earth_application: Improves soot control and burner design in terrestrial combustion systems.

source: Gomez et al., 1987, Santoro et al., 1987, Sunderland et al., 1995
finding: At temperatures below 1250 K, soot does not form in hydrocarbon flames.
safety_implication: Low-temperature zones can inhibit soot hazards in spacecraft fires.
evidence: Studies have reported that at temperatures below 1250 K soot does not form (Gomez et al. , 1987, Santoro et al. , 1987, Sunderland et al. , 1995)
earth_application: Controlling soot emissions from industrial burners.

finding: Permanently-blue flames were obtained at low strain rates under 100 s-1 for acetylene, propylene, and butadiene using nitrogen exchange.
safety_implication: Indicates pathways to suppress soot formation in gaseous hydrocarbon combustion.
evidence: Faeth and co-workers applied nitrogen exchange and their data support the above hypothesis in that they were able to obtain permanently-blue flames at low strain rates (<100 s-1 ) for acetylene, propylene and butadiene.
other_measurements: strain rate: <100 s-1
earth_application: Clean combustion design.

finding: Extinction strain rate for methane-air flames with stoichiometric mixture fraction Zst = 0.055 is 393 s-1.
safety_implication: Quantifies flammability limits and resilience of methane-air diffusion flames under varying conditions.
evidence: For example, the measured extinction strain rate Kext for methane-air flames ( Zst = 0.055) is 393 s-1 while for the diluted methane-oxygen flame ( Zst = 0.78) it is 883 s-1.
earth_application: Fire safety and prevention in methane-handling systems.

finding: Extinction strain rate for diluted methane-oxygen flames with Zst = 0.78 is 883 s-1.
safety_implication: Shows how oxygen and diluent shifting affects flame strength and extinction limits.
evidence: while for the diluted methane-oxygen flame ( Zst = 0.78) it is 883 s-1.
earth_application: Industrial oxygen-enriched combustion safety.

finding: The temperature at extinction for a methane-air flame with Zst = 0.55 at extinction strain rate is 1840 K.
safety_implication: Provides baseline extinction thermal limits for spacecraft fire suppression models.
evidence: The temperature at extinction for Fig 1.4a is 1840 K while that of Fig. 1.4b is 1740 K.
earth_application: Improving combustion efficiency and safety limits.

finding: The temperature at extinction for a diluted methane-enriched air flame with Zst = 0.65 at extinction strain rate is 1740 K.
safety_implication: Demonstrates that redesigned flames can sustain stable burning at lower temperatures, reducing NOx and enhancing efficiency.
evidence: The temperature at extinction for Fig 1.4a is 1840 K while that of Fig. 1.4b is 1740 K.
earth_application: Low-NOx burner design.

finding: Spherical microgravity diffusion flame experiments used a 6.4 mm diameter porous sphere supported by a 1.6 mm stainless steel tube at 0.98 bar quiescent ambient gas.
safety_implication: Provides standard benchmark configurations for validating space-based combustion safety models.
evidence: The rig included a windowed pressure vessel and a burner that consisted of a 6.4 mm diameter porous sphere. The sphere was supported and fed by a 1.6 mm stainless steel tube attached with epoxy. All tests were conducted in quiescent ambient gas at 0.98 bar.
earth_application: Foundational diffusion flame research.

finding: Flame (a) (Oxidizer side, Zst = 0.064) has a mass burning rate of 1.51 mg/s, flame diameter of 29.3 mm, raw temperature of 1302 K, and corrected temperature of 1399 K.
safety_implication: Understanding flame structure and temperatures under microgravity helps evaluate fire growth risks for spacecraft materials.
other_measurements: mb: 1.51 mg/s; df: 29.3 mm; Traw: 1302 K; Tcorrected: 1399 K
variables: Reactant mole fractions and convection direction
earth_application: Improves combustion efficiency and pollutant reduction models on Earth.

finding: Flame (b) (Oxidizer side, Zst = 0.78) has a mass burning rate of 0.08 mg/s, flame diameter of 18.8 mm, raw temperature of 1760 K, and corrected temperature of 1923 K.
safety_implication: Identifies soot-free combustion limits critical for detecting fires in microgravity before smoke generation.
other_measurements: mb: 18.6 mg/s; df: 18.8 mm; Traw: 1760 K; Tcorrected: 1923 K
variables: Reactant mole fractions and convection direction
earth_application: Industrial burner safety and emissions reduction.

finding: Flame (c) (Fuel side, Zst = 0.064) exhibits high soot production with a mass burning rate of 22.2 mg/s, flame diameter of 24.7 mm, raw temperature of 1907 K, and corrected temperature of 2111 K.
safety_implication: High soot-producing conditions warn of dense smoke generation that could obscure crew vision and clog spacecraft filtration.
other_measurements: mb: 22.2 mg/s; df: 24.7 mm; Traw: 1907 K; Tcorrected: 2111 K
variables: Reactant mole fractions and convection direction
earth_application: Understanding soot creation in heavy hydrocarbon combustion.

finding: Flame (d) (Fuel side, Zst = 0.78) is a permanently blue flame with a mass burning rate of 5.18 mg/s, flame diameter of 31.3 mm, raw temperature of 1300 K, and corrected temperature of 1385 K.
safety_implication: Demonstrates that high stoichiometric mixture fraction prevents soot even when convection favors soot growth, aiding optical fire detection reliability.
other_measurements: mb: 5.18 mg/s; df: 31.3 mm; Traw: 1300 K; Tcorrected: 1385 K
variables: Reactant mole fractions and convection direction
earth_application: Cleaner burning systems design.

finding: All four evaluated flames shared a uniform adiabatic flame temperature of 2370 K and an ethylene consumption rate of 1.51 mg/s.
safety_implication: Isolates the effects of flame structure and convection direction from thermal energy release rates in spacecraft fire safety analyses.
evidence: The ethylene consumption rate for all flames was held constant at 1.51 mg/s. All four flames have the same adiabatic flame temperature of 2370 K.
other_measurements: Adibatic flame temperature: 2370 K; Ethylene consumption rate: 1.51 mg/s
earth_application: Fundamental combustion control studies.

finding: Flame structure quantified by Zst has a profound effect on soot production, yielding soot-free conditions at high Zst and sooting conditions at low Zst regardless of convection direction.
safety_implication: Enables better prediction of whether specific fuel-oxidizer combinations will produce hazardous smoke in spacecraft atmospheres.
evidence: The main conclusion of this paper was that flame structure, quantified by Zst, had a profound effect on soot production. Soot-free conditions were observed at high Zst and sooting conditions were observed at low Zst regardless of convection direction.
earth_application: Soot mitigation in practical combustors.

finding: Seventeen sooting limits were identified for spherical diffusion flames covering normal and inverse configurations across a wide range of reactant mole fractions, Zst, and Tad.
safety_implication: Provides a comprehensive database for establishing spacecraft material flammability limits and smoke thresholds.
evidence: Seventeen sooting limits were identified. Normal and inverse flames were represented, with a wide range of reactant mole fractions, Zst, and Tad.
