finding: Flames with residence times in excess of 0.5 s exhibited large gas-phase radiative losses resulting in a significant reduction of peak temperature below the adiabatic flame temperature.
safety_implication: Understanding radiation-induced temperature reductions helps in predicting flame behavior and thermal hazards in spacecraft fire safety design.
evidence: Among the present flames these have the longest residence times (all in excess of 0.5 s) and the most unsteady diameters. These conditions also are associated with large gas-phase radiative losses, leading to a large reduction of actual peak temperature below Tad .
fuel_geometry: Spherical diffusion flame on a porous spherical burner
other_measurements: peak temperature reduction: 970 K
earth_application: Applicable to combustion modeling and radiative heat loss assessments in low-speed or buoyancy-free terrestrial flames.

finding: Convection direction has no measurable effect on the sooting limits of spherical flames.
safety_implication: Demonstrates that gravitational convection orientation does not alter sooting boundaries in spherical configurations, simplifying microgravity combustion risk assessments.
evidence: Figure 1.7 shows that convection direction has no measurable effect on the sooting limits of these spherical flames.
earth_application: Aids in understanding sooting behaviors across different orientations in reduced gravity versus standard gravity.

finding: Thermocouple measurements in the 5 s drop facility confirmed no significant increase in burner surface temperature during the drop, allowing Tb to be taken as a constant 300 K.
safety_implication: Validates thermal boundary conditions for short-duration drop tower experiments used to study spacecraft fire hazards.
evidence: Because thermocouple measurements in the 5 s drop facility showed no significant increase in burner surface temperature during the drop, Tb was taken to be constant at 300 K.
other_measurements: burner temperature: 300 K
earth_application: Improves experimental control and thermal boundary modeling in drop tower combustion facilities.

finding: Flames (b) and (c) approached steady state more rapidly than flames (a) and (d) due to their high flow velocities and low residence times.
safety_implication: Flow velocity and residence time critically dictate how quickly a diffusion flame reaches steady-state behavior in spacecraft environments.
evidence: All four flames initially grew with time, but flames (b) and (c) approached steady state more rapidly than flames (a) and (d) because of their high flow velocities and low residence times.
earth_application: Applicable to industrial burner dynamics and flame stabilization under forced flow.

finding: Peak temperatures of spherical ethylene diffusion flames decreased with time due to gaseous radiative heat loss, except near ignition.
safety_implication: Radiative heat loss mechanisms are vital for predicting temperature decay and thermal loads from sustained fires in spacecraft cabins.
evidence: Due to gaseous radiative heat loss the peak temperatures decrease with time except near ignition.
earth_application: Improves modeling of radiative cooling and thermal structure in large-scale fire propagation.

finding: Low flow velocities and long residence times in the studied diffusion flames enhanced diffusive effects, demonstrating that ambient gas Lewis number significantly affects flame temperature.
safety_implication: Transport properties and Lewis number variations must be accurately accounted for when predicting flame temperatures and flammability limits in microgravity spacecraft environments.
evidence: In summary, this manuscript found that the low flow velocities and long residence times in these diffusion flames lead to enhanced diffusive effects. For example, the results show that the ambient gas Lewis number can have a strong effect on flame temperature – a 10% decrease in Lewis number can increase the steady-state flame temperature by 200 K.
other_measurements: Steady-state flame temperature increase: 200 K for a 10% decrease in Lewis number
earth_application: Relevant to diffusion flame stability, burner design, and combustion kinetics under low-strain conditions.

finding: Transient predictions of flame sizes were significantly larger than those observed in microgravity experiments unless thermal and mass diffusion properties were increased by 30%.
safety_implication: Model inaccuracies in predicting transient flame sizes in micro-g can compromise spacecraft fire growth predictions and hazard assessments.
evidence: Transient predictions of flame sizes were significantly larger than those observed in microgravity experiments. Agreement could not be obtained unless the model’s thermal and mass diffusion properties were increased by 30%.

finding: Two modes of extinction onset were observed in microgravity spherical diffusion flames: base extinction and hole extinction.
safety_implication: Understanding extinction modes helps define flammability boundaries and identify conditions under which fires self-extinguish or persist in spacecraft environments.
evidence: Two modes of extinction onset were observed: base and hole extinction. Base extinction, typically observed at small flowrates, started at the base of the flame near the burner supply tube. Hole extinction, typically observed at high flowrates, started as a flame hole in the blue flame sheet at a distance away from the burner tube.

finding: Base extinction for propane flowing into air at 0.75 mg/s occurred at about 1.4 s both with and without a heating wire, indicating time to extinction is not significantly influenced by heat loss to the burner supply tube.
safety_implication: Burner thermal boundary conditions do not dominate the base extinction phenomenon for these micro-g spherical diffusion flames.
evidence: Figure 1.10 illustrates base extinction for propane flowing into air at 0.75 mg/s with and without the heating wire. Extinction occurs near the burner supply tube at about 1.4 s for both cases, indicating that the time to extinction is not significantly influenced by heat loss to the burner supply tube.
other_measurements: extinction time: 1.4 s

finding: Microgravity diffusion flames exhibited an extinction temperature of about 1100 K, which is significantly lower than normal-gravity hydrocarbon flames.
safety_implication: Lower extinction temperatures in microgravity mean that fires can sustain themselves under conditions where 1-g flames would have already extinguished via radiative heat loss.
evidence: The present results indicate an extinction temperature of about 1100 K for the present flames. This is lower than past measurements of this property in normal-gravity flames (Quintiere 2006).
earth_application: Provides insight into low-temperature extinction limits applicable to low-momentum or quiescent fires on Earth.

evidence: For sooting limit flames with sufficiently long flow times (i.e., above 0.5 s) a common observation observed for all flames, despite their disparate characteristics, was that soot does not exist unless there is a location in the flame where the C/O ratio exceeds 0.51 and the temperature exceeds 1410 K.

earth_application: Improves particulate emissions modeling and soot control in combustion devices and accidental fires.
